name: ABS
purpose: Gives the size of a number without its minus sign.

args.name: number
args.desc: The number or cell whose positive value you want.

example.explain: Shows the budget variance for travel as a positive amount, whether the spend was over or under budget.

tip: Use ABS when you care about the size of a gap, not its direction, such as forecast error.

name: ACCRINT
purpose: Works out the interest that has built up on a bond that pays interest at regular intervals.
syntax: ACCRINT(issue, first_interest, settlement, rate, par, frequency, [basis], [calc_method])

args.name: first_interest
args.desc: Date of the first interest payment.

args.name: basis
args.desc: Day count method, 0 (30/360) if left out.

args.name: calc_method
args.desc: TRUE to count from the issue date, FALSE from the last coupon date.

example.explain: Finds the interest accrued on a ₹1 lakh, 7.5% bond bought three months after issue.

tip: Enter dates with DATE or real date cells; dates typed as text give #VALUE!.

name: ACCRINTM
purpose: Works out the interest built up on a security that pays all its interest at maturity.

args.name: basis
args.desc: Day count method, 0 if left out.

example.explain: Calculates six months of 7% interest on a ₹1 lakh security paid in one go at maturity.

name: ACOS
purpose: Gives the angle, in radians, whose cosine is the number you supply.

example.explain: Returns the angle in radians whose cosine is 0.5, which is 60 degrees.

tip: Wrap it in DEGREES to see the answer in degrees.

name: ACOSH
purpose: Gives the inverse hyperbolic cosine of a number.

args.name: number
args.desc: Any number equal to or greater than 1.

example.explain: Returns the inverse hyperbolic cosine of 2.

name: ACOT
purpose: Gives the angle, in radians, whose cotangent is the number you supply.

example.explain: Returns the angle whose cotangent is 1, which is 45 degrees in radians.

name: ACOTH
purpose: Gives the inverse hyperbolic cotangent of a number.

args.name: number
args.desc: A number whose absolute value is greater than 1.

example.explain: Returns the inverse hyperbolic cotangent of 2.

name: ADDRESS
purpose: Builds a cell address as text from a row number and a column number.

args.name: abs_num
args.desc: 1 for $A$1 style (default), 2, 3 or 4 for relative parts.

args.name: a1
args.desc: TRUE for A1 style (default), FALSE for R1C1 style.

args.name: sheet_text
args.desc: Sheet name to put in front of the address.

example.explain: Turns row 5 and column 3 into the relative address C5.

tip: Pair ADDRESS with INDIRECT to turn the text into a live reference.

name: AGGREGATE
purpose: Runs SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, LARGE and other summaries while choosing to skip hidden rows or error values.
syntax: AGGREGATE(function_num, options, ref1, [ref2], ...) or AGGREGATE(function_num, options, array, [k])

args.name: function_num
args.desc: Which calculation to run: 1 AVERAGE, 2 COUNT, 3 COUNTA, 4 MAX, 5 MIN, 6 PRODUCT, 9 SUM, 12 MEDIAN, 14 LARGE, 15 SMALL and others up to 19.

args.name: options
args.desc: What to ignore: 6 skips errors, 5 skips hidden rows, 7 skips both.

args.name: ref2, ... or k
args.desc: More ranges, or the k position for LARGE, SMALL, PERCENTILE and QUARTILE.

example.explain: Adds branch sales while skipping the #N/A error in Nashik, which would break a plain SUM.

tip: Function numbers 14 to 19 need the array form with k, for example =AGGREGATE(14,6,B2:B5,1) for the top value ignoring errors.

name: AMORDEGRC
purpose: Gives depreciation for each accounting period using a coefficient, as in the French accounting system.
syntax: AMORDEGRC(cost, date_purchased, first_period, salvage, period, rate, [basis])

args.name: first_period
args.desc: End date of the first period.

args.name: salvage
args.desc: Value at the end of its life.

example.explain: Calculates the second-year depreciation on a ₹2.4 lakh machine under the French coefficient method.

tip: Indian books normally use SLN or DB instead; this function follows French rules.

name: AMORLINC
purpose: Gives straight-line depreciation for each accounting period, as in the French accounting system.
syntax: AMORLINC(cost, date_purchased, first_period, salvage, period, rate, [basis])

args.name: first_period
args.desc: End date of the first period.

args.name: salvage
args.desc: Value at the end of its life.

example.explain: Finds the straight-line depreciation for the second period on a ₹2.4 lakh asset at 15%.

tip: For everyday straight-line depreciation SLN is simpler.

name: AND
purpose: Returns TRUE only when every condition you give is TRUE.

example.explain: Checks whether Priya hit ₹1 lakh in sales and 90% attendance, the two bonus conditions.

tip: AND is usually placed inside IF, as in =IF(AND(...),"Bonus","No bonus").

name: ARABIC
purpose: Converts a Roman numeral into an ordinary number.

example.explain: Converts the Roman numeral MMXXVI into 2026.

name: AREAS
purpose: Counts how many separate areas a reference contains.

args.name: reference
args.desc: A cell, range or several ranges in brackets.

example.explain: Counts the two separate ranges inside the brackets.

tip: Put several ranges in an extra pair of brackets so Excel reads them as one argument.

name: ARRAYTOTEXT
purpose: Turns a range or array into a single piece of text.

args.name: array
args.desc: The range or array to convert.

args.name: format
args.desc: 0 for a concise list (default), 1 for strict format with braces and quotes.

example.explain: Joins the three city names into one comma-separated text.

tip: For your own separator or to skip blanks use TEXTJOIN instead.

name: ASC
purpose: Changes full-width (double-byte) characters to half-width characters.

args.name: text
args.desc: Text or a cell containing text.

example.result: EXCEL (with a Japanese, Chinese or Korean editing language; otherwise unchanged)
example.explain: Converts full-width letters, common in East Asian data, into normal width letters; Excel only does this when a double-byte editing language is installed.

tip: Mostly useful for data from East Asian systems; English text is returned unchanged.

name: ASIN
purpose: Gives the angle, in radians, whose sine is the number you supply.

example.explain: Returns 30 degrees, expressed in radians.

tip: Use DEGREES(ASIN(x)) to get degrees.

name: ASINH
purpose: Gives the inverse hyperbolic sine of a number.

example.explain: Returns the inverse hyperbolic sine of 1.

name: ATAN
purpose: Gives the angle, in radians, whose tangent is the number you supply.

example.explain: Returns 45 degrees in radians.

tip: Use ATAN2 when you have x and y coordinates so the quadrant is correct.

name: ATAN2
purpose: Gives the angle, in radians, from the x axis to a point with given x and y coordinates.

example.explain: Finds the angle to the point (4, 3), about 36.9 degrees, in radians.

tip: Excel puts x first, unlike many programming languages which put y first.

name: ATANH
purpose: Gives the inverse hyperbolic tangent of a number.

args.name: number
args.desc: A number between -1 and 1, not including them.

example.explain: Returns the inverse hyperbolic tangent of 0.5.

name: AVEDEV
purpose: Gives the average distance of each value from the mean of the set.

example.explain: Shows that delivery times are, on average, 2 days away from the 7-day mean.

tip: STDEV.S is the more common spread measure; AVEDEV is easier to explain to non-statisticians.

name: AVERAGE
purpose: Gives the arithmetic mean of a set of numbers.

args.name: number2, ...
args.desc: More numbers or ranges, up to 255.

example.explain: Gives the average monthly sales for the first four months of the financial year.

tip: Blank cells are skipped but zeros are counted, so a 0 for a month with no data pulls the average down.

name: AVERAGEA
purpose: Averages values while counting text as 0 and TRUE as 1.

example.explain: Treats the Absent entry as zero, so the average covers all three trainees.

tip: Plain AVERAGE would ignore the text and give 75 instead.

name: AVERAGEIF
purpose: Averages only the cells that meet one condition.

args.name: range
args.desc: Cells to test against the condition.

args.name: average_range
args.desc: Cells to average, if different from range.

example.explain: Averages sales for the North region only.

tip: Point the criteria at a cell, such as =AVERAGEIF(A2:A5,E1,B2:B5), so you can change the region without editing the formula.

name: AVERAGEIFS
purpose: Averages only the cells that meet several conditions at once.

example.explain: Averages North region sales for April only.

tip: The average range comes first in AVERAGEIFS but last in AVERAGEIF, a common mix-up.

name: BAHTTEXT
purpose: Writes a number out in Thai words with the word Baht.

example.result: หนึ่งพันสองร้อยสามสิบสี่บาทถ้วน
example.explain: Writes 1,234 Baht in Thai words.

tip: There is no built-in rupees-in-words function; Indian invoices use a LAMBDA, VBA or the course's amount-in-words formula instead.

name: BASE
purpose: Converts a number into text in another number base, such as binary or hexadecimal.

args.name: number
args.desc: A whole number of 0 or more.

args.name: radix
args.desc: The base to convert to, from 2 to 36.

args.name: min_length
args.desc: Minimum length; pads with leading zeros.

example.explain: Writes 10 in binary, padded to 8 digits.

name: BESSELI
purpose: Gives the modified Bessel function In(x), used in engineering calculations.

args.name: x
args.desc: The value at which to evaluate the function.

args.name: n
args.desc: The order of the function, a whole number.

example.explain: Evaluates the first-order modified Bessel function at 1.5.

name: BESSELJ
purpose: Gives the Bessel function Jn(x), used in engineering calculations.

args.name: x
args.desc: The value at which to evaluate the function.

example.explain: Evaluates the second-order Bessel function at 1.9.

name: BESSELK
purpose: Gives the modified Bessel function Kn(x), used in engineering calculations.

args.name: x
args.desc: The value at which to evaluate the function.

example.explain: Evaluates the first-order modified Bessel function K at 1.5.

name: BESSELY
purpose: Gives the Bessel function Yn(x), also called the Weber or Neumann function.

args.name: x
args.desc: The value at which to evaluate the function.

example.explain: Evaluates the first-order Bessel function Y at 2.5.

name: BETA.DIST
purpose: Gives the beta distribution, often used to model percentages such as task completion.

args.name: cumulative
args.desc: TRUE (or 1) for the cumulative probability, FALSE (or 0) for the density.

example.explain: Gives the cumulative beta probability at 2 for a distribution between 1 and 3.

tip: Used in PERT project estimates, where task time follows a beta shape.

name: BETA.INV
purpose: Gives the value for a given cumulative beta probability.

example.explain: Reverses BETA.DIST and returns the value 2.

name: BETADIST
purpose: Gives the cumulative beta probability (older version kept for compatibility).

example.explain: Gives the cumulative beta probability at 0.4 on the default 0 to 1 scale.

tip: Use BETA.DIST in new workbooks.

name: BETAINV
purpose: Gives the inverse of the cumulative beta distribution (older version kept for compatibility).

example.explain: Returns the value whose cumulative beta probability is about 0.6855.

tip: Use BETA.INV in new workbooks.

name: BIN2DEC
purpose: Converts a binary number into a decimal number.

args.name: number
args.desc: Binary number of up to 10 digits.

example.explain: Converts binary 1100100 into 100.

name: BIN2HEX
purpose: Converts a binary number into hexadecimal.

args.name: number
args.desc: Binary number of up to 10 digits.

args.name: places
args.desc: Number of characters to pad to.

example.explain: Converts binary 11111011 into hexadecimal, padded to 4 characters.

name: BIN2OCT
purpose: Converts a binary number into octal.

args.name: number
args.desc: Binary number of up to 10 digits.

args.name: places
args.desc: Number of characters to pad to.

example.explain: Converts binary 1001 into octal 11, padded to 3 characters.

name: BINOM.DIST
purpose: Gives the probability of a given number of successes in a fixed number of yes or no trials.

args.name: probability_s
args.desc: Chance of success on each trial.

args.name: cumulative
args.desc: TRUE (or 1) for at most that many successes, FALSE (or 0) for exactly that many.

example.explain: Gives the chance of closing exactly 6 sales from 10 calls when each call has a 50% chance.

tip: Switch the last argument to TRUE to get the chance of 6 or fewer.

name: BINOM.DIST.RANGE
purpose: Gives the probability that the number of successes falls within a range.

args.name: probability_s
args.desc: Chance of success on each trial.

args.name: number_s2
args.desc: Highest number of successes; if left out, exactly number_s.

example.explain: Gives the chance that 45 to 50 of 60 customers renew when each renews with a 75% chance.

name: BINOM.INV
purpose: Gives the smallest number of successes for which the cumulative binomial probability reaches a target.

args.name: probability_s
args.desc: Chance of success on each trial.

example.explain: Finds the smallest number of successes out of 6 trials whose cumulative probability is at least 75%.

name: BINOMDIST
purpose: Gives the binomial probability (older version kept for compatibility).

args.name: probability_s
args.desc: Chance of success on each trial.

args.name: cumulative
args.desc: TRUE (or 1) for cumulative, FALSE (or 0) for exact.

example.explain: Gives the chance of exactly 6 successes in 10 trials at 50%.

tip: Use BINOM.DIST in new workbooks.

name: BITAND
purpose: Gives the bitwise AND of two numbers.

example.explain: Keeps only the bits set in both 13 and 25.

name: BITLSHIFT
purpose: Shifts the bits of a number to the left.

example.explain: Shifts 4 two places to the left, which multiplies it by 4.

name: BITOR
purpose: Gives the bitwise OR of two numbers.

example.explain: Combines the bits set in either 23 or 10.

name: BITRSHIFT
purpose: Shifts the bits of a number to the right.

example.explain: Shifts 13 two places to the right, dropping the last two bits.

name: BITXOR
purpose: Gives the bitwise exclusive OR of two numbers.

example.explain: Keeps the bits set in 5 or 3 but not in both.

name: BYCOL
purpose: Runs a LAMBDA calculation on each column of a range and returns one result per column.

args.name: array
args.desc: The range to process column by column.

args.name: lambda
args.desc: A LAMBDA with one parameter for the column, such as LAMBDA(c, SUM(c)). Required; leaving it out gives #CALC!.

example.explain: Totals each month's column and spills the three totals across a row.

tip: In current Microsoft 365 you can pass a function name directly, as in =BYCOL(A2:C3,SUM).

name: BYROW
purpose: Runs a LAMBDA calculation on each row of a range and returns one result per row.

args.name: array
args.desc: The range to process row by row.

args.name: lambda
args.desc: A LAMBDA with one parameter for the row, such as LAMBDA(r, SUM(r)). Required; leaving it out gives #CALC!.

example.explain: Gives each salesperson's quarter total in one spilled column.

tip: A normal SUM copied down does the same job; BYROW shines when the row result must feed another array formula.

name: CALL
purpose: Calls a procedure in a Windows DLL or code resource directly from a cell.

args.name: register_id
args.desc: The ID returned by REGISTER or REGISTER.ID, or the module and procedure names.

example.result: not available (Windows only, blocked by default)
example.explain: Would call a Windows system DLL; it does not work on a Mac and modern Excel blocks it for security.

tip: Treat any workbook that uses CALL with suspicion; use VBA or Office Scripts for automation instead.

name: CEILING
purpose: Rounds a number up to the nearest multiple you choose (older version kept for compatibility).

args.name: significance
args.desc: The multiple to round up to.

example.explain: Rounds a ₹247 price up to the next ₹10.

tip: Use CEILING.MATH in new workbooks; it handles negative numbers more predictably.

name: CEILING.MATH
purpose: Rounds a number up to the nearest whole number or to the nearest multiple you choose.

args.name: significance
args.desc: The multiple to round to, 1 if left out.

args.name: mode
args.desc: For negative numbers: 0 rounds toward zero, any other value rounds away from zero.

example.explain: Rounds 47 units up to whole cartons of 12, so you order 48 units.

tip: Divide instead of rounding if you want the number of cartons: =CEILING.MATH(A2/B2) gives 4.

name: CEILING.PRECISE
purpose: Rounds a number up to the nearest multiple, always toward the higher value whatever its sign.

args.name: significance
args.desc: The multiple to round to, 1 if left out.

example.explain: Rounds minus 247 up to the higher multiple of 10, which is minus 240.

tip: CEILING.MATH with default mode gives the same answer and is easier to remember.

name: CELL
purpose: Returns information about a cell, such as its address, column, format or file name.

args.name: info_type
args.desc: What you want to know, such as "address", "col", "row", "format", "contents" or "filename".

args.name: reference
args.desc: The cell to ask about; if left out, the last changed cell.

example.explain: Returns the address of the cell holding the pen rate.

tip: Always give the reference; without it CELL reports the last edited cell and changes unexpectedly.

name: CHAR
purpose: Returns the character for a given code number.

example.explain: Returns the letter A, which has code 65.

tip: CHAR(10) adds a line break inside a joined text; turn on Wrap Text to see it.

name: CHIDIST
purpose: Gives the right-tailed chi-squared probability (older version kept for compatibility).

example.explain: Gives the probability of a chi-squared value above 18.307 with 10 degrees of freedom.

tip: Use CHISQ.DIST.RT in new workbooks.

name: CHIINV
purpose: Gives the inverse of the right-tailed chi-squared probability (older version kept for compatibility).

example.explain: Returns the chi-squared critical value at 5% with 10 degrees of freedom.

tip: Use CHISQ.INV.RT in new workbooks.

name: CHISQ.DIST
purpose: Gives the left-tailed chi-squared distribution.

args.name: cumulative
args.desc: TRUE (or 1) for cumulative, FALSE (or 0) for density.

example.explain: Gives the probability of a chi-squared value up to 0.5 with 1 degree of freedom.

name: CHISQ.DIST.RT
purpose: Gives the right-tailed chi-squared probability.

example.explain: Gives the chance of a chi-squared value above 18.307 with 10 degrees of freedom.

name: CHISQ.INV
purpose: Gives the inverse of the left-tailed chi-squared distribution.

example.explain: Returns the chi-squared value below which 93% of the distribution lies, with 1 degree of freedom.

name: CHISQ.INV.RT
purpose: Gives the inverse of the right-tailed chi-squared probability, the usual critical value.

example.explain: Returns the 5% critical value with 10 degrees of freedom.

name: CHISQ.TEST
purpose: Tests whether observed counts differ from expected counts and returns the p-value.

example.explain: Tests whether product choice differs from what was expected across two customer groups.

tip: A p-value below 0.05 usually means the difference is unlikely to be chance.

name: CHITEST
purpose: Gives the chi-squared test p-value (older version kept for compatibility).

example.explain: Runs the same chi-squared test as CHISQ.TEST.

tip: Use CHISQ.TEST in new workbooks.

name: CHOOSE
purpose: Picks a value from a list based on a position number.

args.name: index_num
args.desc: Which item to return, from 1 to 254.

example.explain: Shows the scenario name for scenario number 2.

tip: CHOOSE(MONTH(date),...) is a quick way to map months to Indian FY quarters.

name: CHOOSECOLS
purpose: Returns only the columns you pick from a range, in the order you list them.

args.name: array
args.desc: The range to take columns from.

args.name: col_num1
args.desc: First column number to return; negative counts from the right.

example.explain: Pulls the Sales and Name columns, in that order, into a new spilled table.

tip: Combine with FILTER or SORT to return just the columns your report needs.

name: CHOOSEROWS
purpose: Returns only the rows you pick from a range.

args.name: array
args.desc: The range to take rows from.

args.name: row_num1
args.desc: First row number to return; negative counts from the bottom.

example.explain: Returns the first and the last month's rows.

tip: Negative numbers count from the end, so -1 always gives the latest row.

name: CLEAN
purpose: Removes non-printing characters, such as line breaks and tabs, from text.

args.name: text
args.desc: The text or cell to clean.

example.explain: Strips a hidden tab character that came in from a software export, leaving a clean invoice number.

tip: CLEAN does not remove the non-breaking space (code 160) from web data; use SUBSTITUTE(text,CHAR(160)," ") for that.

name: CODE
purpose: Returns the numeric code of the first character in a text.

args.name: text
args.desc: Text whose first character you want the code for.

example.explain: Returns 82, the code for the capital letter R.

tip: Use CODE(MID(A2,n,1)) to find which odd character is hiding in imported text.

name: COLUMN
purpose: Returns the column number of a cell.

args.name: reference
args.desc: The cell to check; if left out, the cell holding the formula.

example.explain: Returns 3 because Sales sits in column C.

tip: COLUMN()-1 inside VLOOKUP lets the column number grow as you copy a formula across.

name: COLUMNS
purpose: Counts the columns in a range or array.

args.name: array
args.desc: The range or array to count.

example.explain: Counts the four columns in the sales table.

name: COMBIN
purpose: Counts the ways to choose a group of items when order does not matter.

args.name: number_chosen
args.desc: How many are chosen each time.

example.explain: Counts how many different 3-person committees can be formed from 8 team members.

tip: Use PERMUT when the order of selection matters.

name: COMBINA
purpose: Counts the ways to choose items when the same item can be picked more than once.

example.explain: Counts the ways to pick 3 sweets from 4 flavours when repeats are allowed.

name: COMPLEX
purpose: Builds a complex number from a real part and an imaginary part.

example.explain: Creates the complex number 3+4i as text.

name: CONCAT
purpose: Joins text from several cells or whole ranges into one text.

example.explain: Joins first and last name with a space between them.

tip: CONCAT does not add separators; use TEXTJOIN when you need commas between many items.

name: CONCATENATE
purpose: Joins several text items into one (older version of CONCAT).

example.explain: Builds the invoice number INV-0501 from its two parts.

tip: CONCATENATE cannot take a whole range like A2:D2; CONCAT and TEXTJOIN can.

name: CONFIDENCE
purpose: Gives the margin of error for a mean using the normal distribution (older version kept for compatibility).

args.name: alpha
args.desc: Significance level, such as 0.05 for 95% confidence.

example.explain: Gives the 95% margin of error for a sample of 50 with standard deviation 2.5.

tip: Use CONFIDENCE.NORM in new workbooks.

name: CONFIDENCE.NORM
purpose: Gives the margin of error for a mean using the normal distribution.

args.name: alpha
args.desc: Significance level, such as 0.05 for 95% confidence.

example.explain: Shows that the average delivery time from 50 orders is accurate to about 0.69 days either way, at 95% confidence.

tip: Add and subtract the result from the sample mean to get the confidence interval.

name: CONFIDENCE.T
purpose: Gives the margin of error for a mean using Student's t distribution, better for small samples.

example.explain: Gives the 95% margin of error for a sample of 50 with standard deviation 1.

name: CONVERT
purpose: Converts a value from one unit of measurement to another.

args.name: from_unit
args.desc: Unit code you have, such as "km", "kg" or "C".

args.name: to_unit
args.desc: Unit code you want, such as "mi", "lbm" or "F".

example.explain: Converts the 150 km Mumbai to Pune distance into miles for a US client.

tip: Unit codes are case-sensitive: "kg" works but "KG" gives #N/A.

name: COPILOT
purpose: Sent a prompt with cell data to Copilot and returned the AI answer in the cell; retired on 14 September 2026.

args.name: context1
args.desc: Cell or range given to Copilot as context.

args.name: prompt_part2, context2, ...
args.desc: More prompt text and context pairs.

data: Delivery was late but the staff were helpful
example.formula: =COPILOT("Classify this feedback as Positive, Negative or Mixed",A2)
example.explain: Showed how the function classified customer feedback; since its retirement on 14 Sep 2026 (MC1454373) it no longer returns AI answers.

tip: Use Copilot chat, Agent Mode or Claude in Excel for these jobs now, and keep results as plain values you have checked.

name: CORREL
purpose: Measures how strongly two sets of numbers move together, from -1 to 1.

args.name: array2
args.desc: Second set of values, same size.

example.explain: Shows a very strong positive link between monthly ad spend and sales.

tip: Correlation is not causation; a festival month can push up both columns.

name: COS
purpose: Gives the cosine of an angle given in radians.

example.explain: Converts 60 degrees to radians and returns its cosine.

tip: Excel trig functions use radians, so wrap degrees in RADIANS first.

name: COSH
purpose: Gives the hyperbolic cosine of a number.

example.explain: Returns the hyperbolic cosine of 1.

name: COT
purpose: Gives the cotangent of an angle given in radians.

example.explain: Returns the cotangent of 45 degrees.

name: COTH
purpose: Gives the hyperbolic cotangent of a number.

example.explain: Returns the hyperbolic cotangent of 1.

name: COUNT
purpose: Counts the cells that contain numbers.

example.explain: Counts the invoices that have a numeric amount, skipping the Pending text and the blank.

tip: Numbers stored as text are not counted; a low COUNT is a quick sign of a text-number problem.

name: COUNTA
purpose: Counts the cells that are not empty.

example.explain: Counts every filled amount cell, including the Pending text.

tip: A cell with a formula returning "" looks blank but COUNTA still counts it.

name: COUNTBLANK
purpose: Counts the empty cells in a range.

example.explain: Finds the one invoice whose amount has not been entered.

tip: Cells with formulas that return "" are counted as blank too.

name: COUNTIF
purpose: Counts the cells that meet one condition.

example.explain: Counts how many orders have been delivered.

tip: Put operators in quotes and join cell values with &, as in =COUNTIF(C2:C50,">"&F1).

name: COUNTIFS
purpose: Counts the rows that meet several conditions at once.

args.name: criteria_range2, criteria2, ...
args.desc: More range and condition pairs, up to 127.

example.explain: Counts North region reps who sold more than ₹1 lakh.

tip: All ranges must be the same size, or you get #VALUE!.

name: COUPDAYBS
purpose: Counts the days from the start of a bond's coupon period to the settlement date.

args.name: basis
args.desc: Day count method, 0 (30/360) if left out.

example.explain: Counts the days since the last coupon on 15 March for a half-yearly bond.

name: COUPDAYS
purpose: Counts the days in the coupon period that contains the settlement date.

args.name: basis
args.desc: Day count method, 0 if left out.

example.explain: Returns the length of the current half-year coupon period on a 30/360 basis.

name: COUPDAYSNC
purpose: Counts the days from the settlement date to the next coupon date.

args.name: basis
args.desc: Day count method, 0 if left out.

example.explain: Counts the days left until the next coupon on 15 September.

name: COUPNCD
purpose: Returns the next coupon date after the settlement date.

example.explain: Finds the next coupon payment date for a half-yearly bond.

tip: Format the result cell as a date, otherwise you see a serial number.

name: COUPNUM
purpose: Counts the coupons still to be paid between settlement and maturity.

example.explain: Counts the ten half-yearly coupons left until March 2031.

name: COUPPCD
purpose: Returns the coupon date just before the settlement date.

example.explain: Finds the last coupon date before you bought the bond.

name: COVAR
purpose: Gives the population covariance of two data sets (older version kept for compatibility).

example.explain: Measures how ad spend and leads move together across four weeks.

tip: Use COVARIANCE.P in new workbooks.

name: COVARIANCE.P
purpose: Gives the population covariance, the average product of deviations of two data sets.

example.explain: Treats the four weeks as the whole population and measures how the two columns move together.

tip: Covariance depends on units; CORREL gives an easier -1 to 1 scale.

name: COVARIANCE.S
purpose: Gives the sample covariance of two data sets.

example.explain: Treats the four weeks as a sample, dividing by 3 instead of 4.

name: CRITBINOM
purpose: Gives the smallest number of successes whose cumulative binomial probability reaches a target (older version kept for compatibility).

args.name: probability_s
args.desc: Chance of success on each trial.

example.explain: Returns 4, the same answer BINOM.INV gives.

tip: Use BINOM.INV in new workbooks.

name: CSC
purpose: Gives the cosecant of an angle given in radians.

example.explain: Returns the cosecant of 30 degrees.

name: CSCH
purpose: Gives the hyperbolic cosecant of a number.

example.explain: Returns the hyperbolic cosecant of 1.

name: CUBEKPIMEMBER
purpose: Returns a key performance indicator property from an OLAP cube.

args.name: connection
args.desc: Name of the workbook connection to the cube.

args.name: kpi_name
args.desc: Name of the KPI in the cube.

args.name: kpi_property
args.desc: Which part to return: 1 value, 2 goal, 3 status, 4 trend and so on.

args.name: caption
args.desc: Text to show in the cell instead.

example.explain: Would fetch the revenue goal from a connected OLAP cube; it needs an external cube connection, which most Mac setups do not have.

tip: Use it inside CUBEVALUE to get the number; on a Mac, PivotTables or Power BI are usually easier.

name: CUBEMEMBER
purpose: Returns a member or tuple from an OLAP cube, such as one region or one month.

args.name: connection
args.desc: Name of the workbook connection to the cube.

args.name: member_expression
args.desc: The member in cube syntax, such as "[Region].[North]".

args.name: caption
args.desc: Text to show instead of the cube caption.

example.explain: Would pick the North region from a connected cube; it needs an OLAP connection, and the Mac has no Data Model.

tip: Convert a PivotTable to formulas on Windows to see the CUBE functions Excel builds for you.

name: CUBEMEMBERPROPERTY
purpose: Returns a property of a member in an OLAP cube, such as the manager of a store.

args.name: connection
args.desc: Name of the cube connection, as text.

args.name: member_expression
args.desc: The member you want, written as an MDX expression.

args.name: property
args.desc: Name of the property to return.

example.result: The manager's name for the Mumbai store
example.explain: Reads the Manager property of the Mumbai store from a cube connection called SalesCube; it needs a live OLAP connection, so it cannot run in the browser.

tip: On a Mac there is no Data Model, so cube functions only work with an external OLAP server connection.

name: CUBERANKEDMEMBER
purpose: Returns the member at a given rank in a cube set, such as the top-selling product.

args.name: connection
args.desc: Name of the cube connection, as text.

args.name: set_expression
args.desc: A set, usually the result of CUBESET.

args.name: rank
args.desc: Which position to return, 1 for the first.

args.name: caption
args.desc: Text to show in the cell instead of the member name.

example.explain: Builds a set of categories sorted by sales (highest first) and returns the first one; it needs a live OLAP connection called SalesCube.

tip: Combine with ROW() or a helper column of 1 to 10 to build a live top 10 list from a cube.

name: CUBESET
purpose: Defines a set of members from an OLAP cube that other cube functions can use.

args.name: connection
args.desc: Name of the cube connection, as text.

args.name: set_expression
args.desc: MDX expression that returns the set of members.

args.name: sort_order
args.desc: 0 none, 1 ascending, 2 descending, and so on.

example.explain: Creates a set of every region sorted by sales from highest to lowest and shows the caption All regions; it needs a live OLAP connection.

tip: The cell only shows the caption; feed the cell into CUBERANKEDMEMBER or CUBESETCOUNT to use the set.

name: CUBESETCOUNT
purpose: Counts how many items are in a cube set.

args.name: set
args.desc: A set from CUBESET, or a cell that holds one.

example.result: The number of regions in the cube, for example 4
example.explain: Counts the regions returned by CUBESET from a cube connection called SalesCube; it needs a live OLAP connection.

tip: Use the count to know how many CUBERANKEDMEMBER rows a report needs.

name: CUBEVALUE
purpose: Returns a total from an OLAP cube for the members you name.

args.name: connection
args.desc: Name of the cube connection, as text.

args.name: member_expression1
args.desc: A measure or member that filters the total.

example.result: Total North sales from the cube
example.explain: Pulls the Sales measure for the North region from a cube connection called SalesCube; it needs a live OLAP connection.

tip: On Windows you can convert a Data Model PivotTable to CUBEVALUE formulas; Mac has no Data Model, so this only works with external cubes.

name: CUMIPMT
purpose: Adds up the interest paid on a loan between two EMI numbers.
syntax: CUMIPMT(rate, nper, pv, start_period, end_period, type)

args.name: rate
args.desc: Interest rate per period, for example annual rate divided by 12.

args.name: pv
args.desc: Loan amount, as a positive number.

args.name: type
args.desc: 0 if EMIs are paid at month end, 1 if at the start.

example.explain: Shows the total interest paid in the first 12 EMIs of a ₹50 lakh home loan at 8.5% for 20 years; it is negative because it is money going out.

tip: The loan amount must be positive and type cannot be left out, otherwise you get #NUM! or an error.

name: CUMPRINC
purpose: Adds up the principal repaid on a loan between two EMI numbers.
syntax: CUMPRINC(rate, nper, pv, start_period, end_period, type)

args.name: rate
args.desc: Interest rate per period, for example annual rate divided by 12.

args.name: pv
args.desc: Loan amount, as a positive number.

args.name: type
args.desc: 0 if EMIs are paid at month end, 1 if at the start.

example.explain: Shows how much of the ₹50 lakh loan principal is repaid in the first year of EMIs.

tip: CUMIPMT plus CUMPRINC for the same periods equals the total EMIs paid in that period.

name: DATE
purpose: Builds a proper Excel date from separate year, month and day numbers.

args.name: month
args.desc: Month number 1 to 12; larger numbers roll into the next year.

args.name: day
args.desc: Day of the month; larger numbers roll into the next month.

example.explain: Joins the year, month and day columns into the date 1 April 2026, the first day of FY 2026-27.

tip: DATE rolls over, so =DATE(2026,13,1) gives 1 January 2027; handy for adding months safely.

name: DATEDIF
purpose: Counts the complete years, months or days between two dates, ideal for age and service length.

args.name: unit
args.desc: "Y" years, "M" months, "D" days, "YM" months left after years, "MD" days left after months, "YD" days left after years.

example.explain: Counts the completed years of service between joining and exit, the figure used for gratuity eligibility.

tip: DATEDIF does not appear in formula autocomplete, so type it in full; if the start date is later than the end date you get #NUM!.

name: DATEVALUE
purpose: Turns a date typed as text into a real date serial number Excel can calculate with.

args.name: date_text
args.desc: Text that looks like a date, such as "15/08/2026".

example.explain: Converts the text 15/08/2026 into its serial number; format the cell as a date to see 15/08/2026.

tip: The text must follow your Mac's region date order; with India region, DD/MM/YYYY text converts correctly.

name: DAVERAGE
purpose: Averages a column of a list for the rows that match a criteria range.

args.name: database
args.desc: The list including its header row.

args.name: field
args.desc: Column to average, as a header name in quotes or a column number.

args.name: criteria
args.desc: A small range with a header and the condition below it.

example.explain: Averages Sales only for rows where Region is North, using the criteria in D1:D2.

tip: AVERAGEIFS does the same job without a separate criteria range and is easier to read.

name: DAY
purpose: Returns the day of the month, from 1 to 31, from a date.

example.explain: Pulls the day number out of the invoice date 15 August 2026.

tip: If DAY returns a strange number, the cell probably holds text, not a real date.

name: DAYS
purpose: Returns the number of days between two dates.

example.explain: Counts how many days the customer took to pay the invoice.

tip: The end date comes first; swap them and you get a negative number. Simple subtraction B2-A2 gives the same answer.

name: DAYS360
purpose: Counts days between two dates using a 360-day year of twelve 30-day months, as some accounting systems do.

args.name: method
args.desc: FALSE or omitted for the US method, TRUE for the European method.

example.explain: Counts a full financial year as 360 days, the way 30/360 interest calculations do.

tip: Use it only when a bank or bond uses 30/360; for real calendar days use DAYS.

name: DB
purpose: Calculates depreciation for a period using the fixed declining balance (written down value) method.

args.name: salvage
args.desc: Value left at the end of its life.

args.name: month
args.desc: Months used in the first year; 12 if left out.

example.explain: Shows first-year depreciation on a ₹5 lakh machine under the written down value method.

tip: DB rounds the rate to three decimals, so its total may differ slightly from a manual WDV schedule.

name: DBCS
purpose: Converts half-width (single-byte) letters to full-width (double-byte) characters for East Asian text.

args.name: text
args.desc: Text or a cell to convert.

example.explain: On a Mac or PC without an East Asian editing language, DBCS returns the text unchanged; with Japanese or Chinese enabled it returns the full-width letters ＡＢＣ.

tip: You will rarely need this for Indian data; it matters only when working with East Asian systems.

name: DCOUNT
purpose: Counts the numbers in a column of a list for rows that match a criteria range.

args.name: database
args.desc: The list including its header row.

args.name: field
args.desc: Column to count, as a header name or column number.

args.name: criteria
args.desc: A small range with a header and the condition below it.

example.explain: Counts the North rows that have a number in the Sales column.

tip: COUNTIFS is usually simpler; database functions shine when users edit the criteria cells directly.

name: DCOUNTA
purpose: Counts non-blank cells in a column of a list for rows that match a criteria range.

args.name: database
args.desc: The list including its header row.

args.name: field
args.desc: Column to count, as a header name or column number.

args.name: criteria
args.desc: A small range with a header and the condition below it.

example.explain: Counts the reps whose sales are above ₹40,000, using the condition in D1:D2.

tip: Criteria written on the same row are AND conditions; on separate rows they are OR conditions.

name: DDB
purpose: Calculates depreciation for a period using the double declining balance method.

args.name: salvage
args.desc: Value left at the end of its life.

example.explain: Shows first-year depreciation on a ₹5 lakh asset at twice the straight-line rate.

tip: DDB never depreciates below salvage, but it does not switch to straight line on its own; use VDB for that.

name: DEC2BIN
purpose: Converts a decimal number to binary text.

args.name: places
args.desc: Minimum number of characters, padded with zeros.

example.explain: Converts 10 into its binary form 1010.

tip: The result is text, so use BIN2DEC to turn it back into a number.

name: DEC2HEX
purpose: Converts a decimal number to hexadecimal text.

args.name: places
args.desc: Minimum number of characters, padded with zeros.

example.explain: Converts 255 into the hexadecimal code FF, as used in colour codes.

tip: Use places to pad, for example =DEC2HEX(10,2) gives 0A.

name: DEC2OCT
purpose: Converts a decimal number to octal text.

args.name: places
args.desc: Minimum number of characters, padded with zeros.

example.explain: Converts 64 into octal, which is 100.

name: DECIMAL
purpose: Converts a number written in another base, such as hex or binary, into a normal decimal number.

args.name: text
args.desc: The number written in the other base, as text.

example.explain: Reads FF as a base-16 number and returns 255.

tip: BASE does the reverse: decimal to any base.

name: DEGREES
purpose: Converts an angle in radians into degrees.

example.explain: Converts pi radians into 180 degrees.

tip: Excel's SIN, COS and TAN work in radians; use RADIANS to go the other way.

name: DELTA
purpose: Checks whether two numbers are equal and returns 1 if they are, otherwise 0.

args.name: number2
args.desc: The second number; 0 if left out.

example.explain: Returns 1 because actual spend exactly matches the budget; add it down a column to count exact matches.

tip: For everyday checks =A2=B2 returns TRUE or FALSE and is easier to read.

name: DETECTLANGUAGE
purpose: Identifies the language of a piece of text and returns its language code.

args.name: text
args.desc: The text or cell to check.

example.explain: Detects that the feedback is in Hindi and returns the code hi; it needs Microsoft 365 and an internet connection, so the page shows the stored result.

tip: Pair it with TRANSLATE to send only non-English feedback for translation.

name: DEVSQ
purpose: Returns the sum of squared differences of each value from the average.

example.explain: The average is 6, and the squared gaps 4, 1, 4 and 1 add up to 10.

tip: DEVSQ divided by (count minus 1) gives the sample variance, VAR.S.

name: DGET
purpose: Returns the single value from a list that matches a criteria range.

args.name: database
args.desc: The list including its header row.

args.name: field
args.desc: Column to return, as a header name or column number.

args.name: criteria
args.desc: A small range with a header and the condition below it.

example.explain: Finds the row where Rep is Meena and returns her sales.

tip: DGET gives #NUM! if more than one row matches and #VALUE! if none do; XLOOKUP is friendlier.

name: DISC
purpose: Returns the discount rate of a security bought below its redemption value, such as a treasury bill.

args.name: basis
args.desc: Day count method; 0 (30/360) if left out.

example.explain: Works out the annual discount rate on a six-month bill bought at ₹97.50 and redeemed at ₹100.

tip: Use basis 3 (actual/365) to match how Indian T-bills are usually quoted.

name: DMAX
purpose: Returns the largest value in a column of a list for rows that match a criteria range.

args.name: database
args.desc: The list including its header row.

args.name: field
args.desc: Column to check, as a header name or column number.

args.name: criteria
args.desc: A small range with a header and the condition below it.

example.explain: Finds the highest sales among North region reps.

tip: MAXIFS gives the same answer without a criteria range.

name: DMIN
purpose: Returns the smallest value in a column of a list for rows that match a criteria range.

args.name: database
args.desc: The list including its header row.

args.name: field
args.desc: Column to check, as a header name or column number.

args.name: criteria
args.desc: A small range with a header and the condition below it.

example.explain: Finds the lowest sales among North region reps.

tip: MINIFS gives the same answer without a criteria range.

name: DOLLAR
purpose: Turns a number into text formatted as currency with your system's currency symbol.

args.name: decimals
args.desc: Digits after the decimal point; 2 if left out.

example.explain: Formats the amount as rupee text with two decimals; the symbol and grouping follow your Mac's region settings.

tip: The result is text, so it cannot be summed; use a number format if you still need to calculate.

name: DOLLARDE
purpose: Converts a price written as a fraction (like 1.02 meaning 1 and 2/16) into a decimal.

args.name: fractional_dollar
args.desc: Price where the digits after the point are the numerator.

example.explain: Reads 1.02 as 1 and 2/16 and returns 1.125.

tip: Fractional prices are mostly seen in US bond quotes; DOLLARFR does the reverse.

name: DOLLARFR
purpose: Converts a decimal price into the fractional notation used in some bond quotes.

args.name: fraction
args.desc: The denominator to use, such as 16 or 32.

example.explain: Writes 1.125 as 1 and 2/16, shown as 1.02.

name: DPRODUCT
purpose: Multiplies the values in a column of a list for rows that match a criteria range.

args.name: database
args.desc: The list including its header row.

args.name: field
args.desc: Column to multiply, as a header name or column number.

args.name: criteria
args.desc: A small range with a header and the condition below it.

example.explain: Multiplies the quantities of the stationery rows only: 4 x 5 x 3.

tip: Rarely needed; PRODUCT with FILTER does the same in Microsoft 365.

name: DROP
purpose: Removes a number of rows or columns from the start or end of a range and returns the rest.

args.name: array
args.desc: The range or array to trim.

args.name: rows
args.desc: Rows to remove; positive from the top, negative from the bottom.

args.name: columns
args.desc: Columns to remove; positive from the left, negative from the right.

example.explain: Drops the header row and spills the three data rows.

tip: Use a negative number, like DROP(range,-1), to remove a totals row at the bottom.

name: DSTDEV
purpose: Returns the sample standard deviation of a column for rows that match a criteria range.

args.name: database
args.desc: The list including its header row.

args.name: field
args.desc: Column to use, as a header name or column number.

args.name: criteria
args.desc: A small range with a header and the condition below it.

example.explain: Measures how spread out North sales are, treating them as a sample.

tip: STDEV.S with FILTER is the modern way to get the same figure.

name: DSTDEVP
purpose: Returns the population standard deviation of a column for rows that match a criteria range.

args.name: database
args.desc: The list including its header row.

args.name: field
args.desc: Column to use, as a header name or column number.

args.name: criteria
args.desc: A small range with a header and the condition below it.

example.explain: Measures the spread of North sales treating them as the whole population.

tip: Use the P version only when the rows are every value there is, not a sample.

name: DSUM
purpose: Adds the values in a column of a list for rows that match a criteria range.

args.name: database
args.desc: The list including its header row.

args.name: field
args.desc: Column to add, as a header name or column number.

args.name: criteria
args.desc: A small range with a header and the condition below it.

example.explain: Adds up sales for the North region only.

tip: DSUM is handy with OR conditions: put each option on its own row of the criteria range.

name: DURATION
purpose: Returns the Macaulay duration of a bond, the weighted average time in years to receive its cash flows.

args.name: basis
args.desc: Day count method; 0 if left out.

example.explain: Gives the duration in years of a 5-year 7.18% government bond paying half-yearly coupons at a 7.5% yield.

tip: Higher duration means the bond price moves more when interest rates change.

name: DVAR
purpose: Returns the sample variance of a column for rows that match a criteria range.

args.name: database
args.desc: The list including its header row.

args.name: field
args.desc: Column to use, as a header name or column number.

args.name: criteria
args.desc: A small range with a header and the condition below it.

example.explain: Calculates the sample variance of North region sales.

tip: Variance is in squared units; take its square root (DSTDEV) for a figure in rupees.

name: DVARP
purpose: Returns the population variance of a column for rows that match a criteria range.

args.name: database
args.desc: The list including its header row.

args.name: field
args.desc: Column to use, as a header name or column number.

args.name: criteria
args.desc: A small range with a header and the condition below it.

example.explain: Calculates the population variance of North region sales.

tip: Use DVAR instead when the rows are only a sample of all possible values.

name: EDATE
purpose: Returns the date that is a given number of months before or after a start date.

args.name: months
args.desc: Months to add; use a negative number to go back.

example.explain: Finds the renewal date of an insurance policy 12 months after it starts.

tip: EDATE returns a serial number; press ⌘ + 1 and choose a date format if you see something like 46492.

name: EFFECT
purpose: Converts a nominal annual interest rate into the effective annual rate after compounding.

args.name: npery
args.desc: Compounding periods per year, for example 4 for quarterly.

example.explain: Shows that a 7.2% FD compounded quarterly actually earns about 7.40% a year.

tip: Use EFFECT to compare FDs from banks that compound monthly, quarterly or yearly.

name: ENCODEURL
purpose: Converts text into a URL-safe form, replacing spaces and symbols with percent codes.

example.explain: Replaces each space with %20 so the text can go inside a web address; this works only in Excel for Windows.

tip: ENCODEURL does not work on a Mac or in Excel for the web; build such links on Windows or with SUBSTITUTE.

name: EOMONTH
purpose: Returns the last day of the month, a given number of months before or after a date.

args.name: months
args.desc: Months to move; 0 for the same month, negative to go back.

example.explain: Returns the last day of the invoice month, useful for month-end due dates.

tip: =EOMONTH(A2,-1)+1 gives the first day of the same month.

name: ERF
purpose: Returns the error function, used in engineering and statistics.

args.name: upper_limit
args.desc: The upper bound; if left out, integrates from 0 to lower_limit.

example.explain: Returns the error function between 0 and 1.

name: ERF.PRECISE
purpose: Returns the error function from 0 to a given value.

example.explain: Returns the error function between 0 and 1, same as ERF(1).

name: ERFC
purpose: Returns the complementary error function, which is 1 minus ERF.

example.explain: Returns 1 minus ERF(1).

name: ERFC.PRECISE
purpose: Returns the complementary error function, which is 1 minus ERF.

example.explain: Returns the complementary error function at 1.

name: ERROR.TYPE
purpose: Returns a number that tells you which kind of error a value is.

args.name: error_val
args.desc: The value or formula to check.

example.explain: Dividing by zero units gives #DIV/0!, which is error type 2.

tip: Codes: 1 #NULL!, 2 #DIV/0!, 3 #VALUE!, 4 #REF!, 5 #NAME?, 6 #NUM!, 7 #N/A; a non-error returns #N/A.

name: EUROCONVERT
purpose: Converts amounts between the euro and old euro-zone currencies using fixed rates.

args.name: source
args.desc: Three-letter code of the source currency, such as "DEM".

args.name: target
args.desc: Three-letter code of the target currency, such as "EUR".

args.name: triangulation_precision
args.desc: Decimals used in the middle euro step.

example.explain: Converts 1,000 old German marks to euros; it needs the Euro Currency Tools add-in on Windows and does not work on a Mac.

tip: It only covers legacy euro currencies; for rupee rates use the Currencies data type or a rate table.

name: EVEN
purpose: Rounds a number up to the next even whole number.

example.explain: Rounds 23 guests up to 24 so that rooms can be booked on twin sharing.

tip: Negative numbers round away from zero, so EVEN(-3) gives -4.

name: EXACT
purpose: Checks whether two pieces of text are exactly the same, including upper and lower case.

example.explain: Returns FALSE because the case differs, even though =A2=B2 would say TRUE.

tip: Use EXACT to check passwords, product codes or PAN numbers where case matters.

name: EXP
purpose: Returns e (about 2.718) raised to a power, used for continuous growth.

args.name: number
args.desc: The power to raise e to.

example.explain: Grows ₹10,000 at 7% compounded continuously for 5 years.

tip: LN is the reverse of EXP.

name: EXPAND
purpose: Grows a range to a set number of rows and columns, filling new cells with a value you choose.

args.name: array
args.desc: The range or array to grow.

args.name: pad_with
args.desc: Value for the new cells; #N/A if left out.

example.explain: Pads the two quarters to a four-row block, showing a hyphen for Q3 and Q4 until data arrives.

tip: Always give pad_with, otherwise the extra cells show #N/A.

name: EXPON.DIST
purpose: Returns the exponential distribution, used for waiting times between events.

args.name: lambda
args.desc: Average events per unit of time.

args.name: cumulative
args.desc: TRUE for the probability up to x, FALSE for the density.

example.explain: If a call centre gets one call every 5 minutes on average, this is the chance the next call comes within 5 minutes.

name: EXPONDIST
purpose: Returns the exponential distribution (older version kept for compatibility).

args.name: lambda
args.desc: Average events per unit of time.

args.name: cumulative
args.desc: TRUE for the probability up to x, FALSE for the density.

example.explain: Chance that the next call arrives within 5 minutes when calls average one every 5 minutes.

tip: Use EXPON.DIST in new workbooks; EXPONDIST is kept only for old files.

name: F.DIST
purpose: Returns the left-tailed F probability distribution, used to compare two variances.

args.name: cumulative
args.desc: TRUE for the cumulative probability, FALSE for the density.

example.explain: Probability that an F value with 5 and 10 degrees of freedom is 2 or less.

name: F.DIST.RT
purpose: Returns the right-tailed F probability distribution.

example.explain: Probability that an F value with 5 and 10 degrees of freedom is above 2.

name: F.INV
purpose: Returns the inverse of the left-tailed F distribution.

example.explain: Finds the F value below which 95% of the distribution lies.

name: F.INV.RT
purpose: Returns the inverse of the right-tailed F distribution, the usual critical value for an F-test.

example.explain: Gives the critical F value at 5% significance for 5 and 10 degrees of freedom.

name: F.TEST
purpose: Returns the probability that two sets of data have the same variance.

example.explain: Compares how much daily orders vary at the two branches; 0.0212 is below 0.05, so Branch B is significantly more variable.

tip: The result is two-tailed; values below 0.05 usually mean the variances differ.

name: FACT
purpose: Returns the factorial of a number, for example 5! = 120.

args.name: number
args.desc: A whole number 0 or more; decimals are cut off.

example.explain: Counts the ways to order 5 speakers at a conference.

name: FACTDOUBLE
purpose: Returns the double factorial of a number, multiplying every second number.

example.explain: Multiplies 7 x 5 x 3 x 1.

name: FALSE
purpose: Returns the logical value FALSE.

example.explain: Returns the logical value FALSE; typing FALSE in a cell does the same.

tip: In maths FALSE counts as 0, so =FALSE()+1 gives 1.

name: FDIST
purpose: Returns the right-tailed F distribution (older version kept for compatibility).

example.explain: Probability that an F value with 5 and 10 degrees of freedom is above 2.

tip: Use F.DIST.RT in new workbooks; FDIST is kept only for old files.

name: FIELDVALUE
purpose: Pulls one field, such as price or population, out of a linked data type like Stocks or Geography.

args.name: value
args.desc: A cell holding a linked data type.

args.name: field_name
args.desc: The field to return, as text, such as "Price".

example.result: The latest Infosys share price in ₹
example.explain: Once A2 is converted to the Stocks data type, this returns its current price; it needs Microsoft 365 and an internet connection.

tip: The shorter form =A2.Price does the same once the cell is a data type.

name: FILTER
purpose: Returns only the rows of a range that meet the conditions you set.

args.name: include
args.desc: A TRUE or FALSE test with one result per row.

args.name: if_empty
args.desc: What to show if no rows match.

example.explain: Spills the names of reps whose sales are above ₹40,000, and updates by itself when the data changes.

tip: Add a third argument such as "None" to show a message when nothing matches, and join conditions with * for AND or + for OR.

name: FILTERXML
purpose: Extracts values from XML text using an XPath expression.

args.name: xpath
args.desc: The XPath that picks the items to return.

example.explain: Pulls every city element out of the XML and spills them down; this works only in Excel for Windows.

tip: FILTERXML does not work on a Mac; use TEXTSPLIT or TEXTBEFORE/TEXTAFTER to split text there.

name: FIND
purpose: Returns the position of one piece of text inside another, matching upper and lower case exactly.

args.name: start_num
args.desc: Character position to start searching from; 1 if left out.

example.explain: Finds that the @ sign is the 9th character, which you can feed into LEFT to get the user name.

tip: FIND is case-sensitive and gives #VALUE! when nothing is found; use SEARCH for a case-insensitive match.

name: FINDB
purpose: Works like FIND but counts bytes, which matters only for double-byte languages.

args.name: start_num
args.desc: Byte position to start from; 1 if left out.

example.explain: For English text FINDB gives the same answer as FIND.

tip: Only differs from FIND when a double-byte language such as Japanese is set as the editing language.

name: FINV
purpose: Returns the inverse of the right-tailed F distribution (older version kept for compatibility).

example.explain: Gives the critical F value at 5% significance for 5 and 10 degrees of freedom.

tip: Use F.INV.RT in new workbooks; FINV is kept only for old files.

name: FISHER
purpose: Returns the Fisher transformation of a correlation value.

args.name: x
args.desc: A value between -1 and 1, such as a correlation.

example.explain: Transforms a correlation of 0.75 so that it can be tested with normal-distribution methods.

name: FISHERINV
purpose: Reverses the Fisher transformation to get back a correlation value.

example.explain: Turns 0.973 back into a correlation of about 0.75.

name: FIXED
purpose: Rounds a number and returns it as text with a fixed number of decimals and optional commas.

args.name: decimals
args.desc: Digits after the decimal point; 2 if left out.

args.name: no_commas
args.desc: TRUE to leave out the thousands separators.

example.explain: Rounds the amount to whole rupees and puts it inside a sentence with separators.

tip: The digit grouping follows your Mac's region; TEXT gives you full control with a format code.

name: FLOOR
purpose: Rounds a number down to the nearest multiple of a value (older version kept for compatibility).

args.name: significance
args.desc: The multiple to round down to.

example.explain: Rounds ₹1,234 down to the nearest ₹50.

tip: Use FLOOR.MATH in new workbooks; it handles negative numbers more predictably.

name: FLOOR.MATH
purpose: Rounds a number down to the nearest whole number or multiple you choose.

args.name: significance
args.desc: The multiple to round down to; 1 if left out.

args.name: mode
args.desc: For negative numbers, a non-zero value rounds toward zero.

example.explain: Rounds a ₹1,249 price down to the ₹50 slab, useful for discount bands.

tip: FLOOR.MATH changes the value, unlike number formatting, which only changes how it looks.

name: FLOOR.PRECISE
purpose: Rounds a number down to the nearest multiple, always toward minus infinity.

args.name: significance
args.desc: The multiple; 1 if left out. Its sign is ignored.

example.explain: Rounds -7.5 down to -8, the next lower multiple of 2.

tip: FLOOR.MATH does the same by default and is the one to remember.

name: FORECAST
purpose: Predicts a value on a straight-line trend (older version kept for compatibility).

example.explain: Fits a straight line through five months of sales and predicts month 6.

tip: Use FORECAST.LINEAR in new workbooks; FORECAST gives the same result.

name: FORECAST.ETS
purpose: Predicts a future value using exponential smoothing, which can pick up seasonal patterns.

args.name: target_date
args.desc: The date or period to predict.

args.name: timeline
args.desc: Evenly spaced dates or periods for the values.

args.name: seasonality
args.desc: Season length; 1 to detect automatically, 0 for none.

args.name: data_completion
args.desc: 1 fills missing points by averaging, 0 treats them as zero.

args.name: aggregation
args.desc: How to combine duplicate dates; average if left out.

example.explain: Uses exponential smoothing on five months of sales to forecast month 6.

tip: ETS needs a timeline with equal steps; with two or more years of monthly data it can find a 12-month season.

name: FORECAST.ETS.CONFINT
purpose: Returns the plus-or-minus range around an ETS forecast at a chosen confidence level.

args.name: target_date
args.desc: The date or period being forecast.

args.name: confidence_level
args.desc: Confidence between 0 and 1; 0.95 if left out.

example.explain: Gives the margin to add to and subtract from the month 6 forecast for a 95% confidence band.

tip: Forecast plus and minus this value gives the upper and lower lines that Forecast Sheet draws.

name: FORECAST.ETS.SEASONALITY
purpose: Returns the length of the repeating seasonal pattern that Excel detects in your data.

example.explain: Checks five months of sales for a repeating cycle; on such a short series Excel picks up a 2-month zigzag, so always sanity check the detected season.

tip: A result of 12 on monthly data means Excel found a yearly pattern.

name: FORECAST.ETS.STAT
purpose: Returns one of the statistics behind an ETS forecast, such as the smoothing factor or error.

args.name: statistic_type
args.desc: 1 to 8, for example 1 alpha, 5 MAPE, 8 RMSE.

example.explain: Returns the RMSE, the typical size of the forecast error, here about ₹1 thousand.

tip: Compare MAPE (type 5) across models to pick the more accurate forecast.

name: FORECAST.LINEAR
purpose: Predicts a future value by fitting a straight line through past data.

args.name: x
args.desc: The period or input to predict for.

args.name: known_y's
args.desc: The past values, such as sales.

example.explain: Fits a straight trend line through five months of sales and projects month 6 at ₹155 thousand.

tip: The y values come before the x values; swapping them gives a very different answer.

name: FORMULATEXT
purpose: Shows the formula in a cell as text.

args.name: reference
args.desc: The cell whose formula you want to see.

example.explain: Displays the GST formula from B2 next to its result, handy for training sheets.

tip: Returns #N/A if the cell has no formula; ⌘ + ` shows all formulas at once instead.

name: FREQUENCY
purpose: Counts how many values fall into each band you define and returns the counts as a list.

args.name: bins_array
args.desc: The upper limit of each band, in ascending order.

example.explain: Counts salaries up to ₹30,000, from ₹30,001 to ₹50,000, and above ₹50,000; the result has one extra row for the top band.

tip: The output is always one row longer than the bins, for values above the last limit.

name: FTEST
purpose: Returns the result of an F-test on two data sets (older version kept for compatibility).

example.explain: Tests whether the two branches have similar variation in daily orders; 0.0212 is below 0.05, so they likely differ.

tip: Use F.TEST in new workbooks; FTEST is kept only for old files.

name: FV
purpose: Returns the future value of regular investments or a lump sum, such as a SIP or RD maturity amount.

args.name: rate
args.desc: Interest rate per period, for example annual return divided by 12.

args.name: pmt
args.desc: Amount invested each period, entered as negative.

args.name: pv
args.desc: Lump sum invested at the start, entered as negative.

args.name: type
args.desc: 0 for end of period, 1 for start of period.

example.explain: Shows that a ₹5,000 monthly SIP grows to about ₹11.5 lakh in 10 years at 12% a year.

tip: Money you pay out is negative; put a minus sign before the SIP amount to get a positive result.

name: FVSCHEDULE
purpose: Returns the future value of a sum after applying a different interest rate each period.

args.name: schedule
args.desc: The list of rates, one per period.

example.explain: Grows ₹1 lakh through three years of FD renewals at 7%, 7.5% and 8%.

tip: Useful when rates change at each renewal, which FV cannot handle.

name: GAMMA
purpose: Returns the gamma function value, an extension of the factorial.

args.name: number
args.desc: A number that is not zero or a negative whole number.

example.explain: GAMMA(5) equals 4!, which is 24.

name: GAMMA.DIST
purpose: Returns the gamma distribution, used for waiting times and skewed data.

args.name: cumulative
args.desc: TRUE for the cumulative probability, FALSE for the density.

example.explain: Probability that a gamma variable with shape 3 and scale 2 is 10 or less.

name: GAMMA.INV
purpose: Returns the inverse of the gamma cumulative distribution.

example.explain: Finds the median of a gamma distribution with shape 3 and scale 2.

name: GAMMADIST
purpose: Returns the gamma distribution (older version kept for compatibility).

args.name: cumulative
args.desc: TRUE for cumulative, FALSE for density.

example.explain: Same result as GAMMA.DIST with the same inputs.

tip: Use GAMMA.DIST in new workbooks; GAMMADIST is kept only for old files.

name: GAMMAINV
purpose: Returns the inverse gamma distribution (older version kept for compatibility).

example.explain: Same result as GAMMA.INV with the same inputs.

tip: Use GAMMA.INV in new workbooks; GAMMAINV is kept only for old files.

name: GAMMALN
purpose: Returns the natural logarithm of the gamma function.

example.explain: Returns the natural log of GAMMA(10), which is the log of 9!.

name: GAMMALN.PRECISE
purpose: Returns the natural logarithm of the gamma function.

example.explain: Same as GAMMALN(10).

name: GAUSS
purpose: Returns the probability that a standard normal value falls between the mean and a given number of standard deviations.

args.name: z
args.desc: Number of standard deviations from the mean.

example.explain: About 34.13% of normally distributed values lie between the mean and one standard deviation above it.

tip: GAUSS(z) equals NORM.S.DIST(z,TRUE) minus 0.5.

name: GCD
purpose: Returns the greatest common divisor of two or more whole numbers.

example.explain: Finds that 12 identical gift kits can be made from 48 pens and 36 notebooks with nothing left over.

name: GEOMEAN
purpose: Returns the geometric mean, the right way to average growth rates.

example.explain: Averages yearly growth of 10%, 5% and 20% correctly, giving a compound annual growth of about 11.49%.

tip: Enter growth as factors (1.10, not 10%), because GEOMEAN cannot take zero or negative values.

name: GESTEP
purpose: Returns 1 if a number is greater than or equal to a threshold, otherwise 0.

example.explain: Returns 1 because the rep met the target; summing a column of these counts achievers.

tip: =--(A2>=B2) or an IF gives the same result and is easier for colleagues to read.

name: GETPIVOTDATA
purpose: Pulls a specific value out of a PivotTable so your report keeps working when the pivot changes shape.

args.name: data_field
args.desc: Name of the value field, in quotes.

args.name: field1, item1, ...
args.desc: Pairs of field name and item that pick the value.

example.result: Total North sales shown in the PivotTable
example.explain: Returns the North total from a PivotTable that starts at A3; it needs a real PivotTable, so the page shows a description.

tip: Typing = and clicking a pivot cell writes this formula for you; turn that off under PivotTable Analyze > Options if you prefer plain references.

name: GROUPBY
purpose: Groups rows by one or more fields and summarises values with a single formula.

args.name: row_fields
args.desc: Column or columns to group by.

args.name: function
args.desc: How to summarise, such as SUM, AVERAGE or COUNTA.

args.name: field_headers
args.desc: Whether the ranges include headers and whether to show them.

args.name: total_depth
args.desc: 0 no totals, 1 grand total, 2 subtotals too.

args.name: sort_order
args.desc: Column number to sort by; negative for descending.

args.name: filter_array
args.desc: TRUE or FALSE per row to include it.

args.name: field_relationship
args.desc: How multiple row fields relate: 0 hierarchy, 1 table.

example.explain: Builds a region-wise sales summary with a grand total, like a small PivotTable that updates by itself.

tip: Use a negative sort_order such as -2 to list the biggest region first.

name: GROWTH
purpose: Predicts values along an exponential growth curve fitted to your data.

args.name: const
args.desc: FALSE to force the curve through 1.

example.explain: Users grow 20% a year, so the exponential trend predicts 207.36 for year 5.

tip: Use TREND for straight-line growth and GROWTH for percentage growth.

name: HARMEAN
purpose: Returns the harmonic mean, used to average rates such as speeds or price per unit.

example.explain: A delivery van going 40 km/h one way and 60 km/h back averages 48 km/h, not 50.

tip: Use it when averaging rates over the same distance or the same amount spent.

name: HEX2BIN
purpose: Converts a hexadecimal number into its binary form.

args.name: number
args.desc: The hexadecimal value to convert, as text such as "1F".

args.name: places
args.desc: How many characters to show, padded with leading zeros.

example.explain: Turns the hex code 1F into binary, which is 11111.

tip: Inputs above hex 1FF or below FFFFFFFE00 give #NUM! because the binary result is limited to 10 characters.

name: HEX2DEC
purpose: Converts a hexadecimal number into an ordinary decimal number.

args.name: number
args.desc: The hexadecimal value to convert, up to 10 characters.

example.explain: Converts the hex value FF, used in colour codes, to the decimal 255.

tip: Handy for splitting web colour codes such as #1F4E79 into red, green and blue values with MID and HEX2DEC.

name: HEX2OCT
purpose: Converts a hexadecimal number into octal.

args.name: places
args.desc: How many characters to show, padded with leading zeros.

example.explain: Converts hex 1F (decimal 31) into octal 37.

name: HLOOKUP
purpose: Looks for a value in the top row of a table and returns a value from a row below it.

args.name: lookup_value
args.desc: What to look for in the first row.

args.name: table_array
args.desc: The table whose first row is searched.

args.name: row_index_num
args.desc: Which row of the table to return from, counting the top row as 1.

args.name: range_lookup
args.desc: FALSE for an exact match, TRUE or left out for the nearest smaller match in a sorted row.

example.explain: Finds May in the month row and returns the sales figure from row 2 of the table.

tip: Always type FALSE as the last argument for exact matches; XLOOKUP does the same job without counting rows.

name: HOUR
purpose: Returns the hour (0 to 23) from a time.

args.name: serial_number
args.desc: The time (or date and time) to read the hour from.

example.explain: Reads the hour part of Priya's 2:45 pm login time.

tip: HOUR never goes above 23, so for total hours worked over 24 use =A2*24 instead.

name: HSTACK
purpose: Joins ranges or arrays side by side into one wider array.

args.name: array1
args.desc: The first range or array to place on the left.

args.name: array2, ...
args.desc: More ranges or arrays to add to the right.

example.explain: Builds a new two-column list with City first and Name second, without copying any cells.

tip: Shorter arrays are padded with #N/A; wrap the formula in IFNA(...,"") to show blanks instead.

name: HYPERLINK
purpose: Creates a clickable link to a web page, a file or a place in the workbook.

args.name: link_location
args.desc: The web address, file path or cell address (start with # for a cell in this file) to open.

args.name: friendly_name
args.desc: The text shown in the cell instead of the address.

example.explain: Shows the words GST portal in the cell, and clicking them opens the GST website.

tip: To jump to a cell in the same workbook use a # address, for example =HYPERLINK("#Summary!A1","Go to Summary").

name: HYPGEOM.DIST
purpose: Gives the probability of getting a set number of successes in a sample drawn without replacement.

args.name: sample_s
args.desc: Number of successes in the sample.

args.name: population_s
args.desc: Number of successes in the whole population.

args.name: cumulative
args.desc: TRUE for 'at most' this many successes, FALSE for exactly this many.

example.explain: Works out the chance that a quality check of 10 items from a lot of 50 (5 faulty) finds exactly one faulty item.

tip: Use it for sampling without putting items back; use BINOM.DIST when each draw is independent.

name: HYPGEOMDIST
purpose: Older version of HYPGEOM.DIST that gives the probability of an exact number of successes in a sample.

args.name: sample_s
args.desc: Number of successes in the sample.

args.name: population_s
args.desc: Number of successes in the population.

example.explain: Gives the chance of finding exactly one faulty item when checking 10 out of a lot of 50 with 5 faulty.

tip: Kept for old files; use HYPGEOM.DIST, which can also return the cumulative probability.

name: IF
purpose: Checks a condition and returns one value when it is true and another when it is false.

args.name: logical_test
args.desc: The condition to check, such as B2>=C2.

args.name: value_if_true
args.desc: What to return when the condition is true.

args.name: value_if_false
args.desc: What to return when the condition is false; FALSE if left out.

example.explain: Checks whether Asha's sales reached her target and shows Bonus because ₹5,20,000 is above ₹5,00,000.

tip: Text results need double quotes, but numbers and cell references do not.

name: IFERROR
purpose: Returns a value you choose when a formula produces any error, otherwise the formula's result.

args.name: value
args.desc: The formula to check for an error.

args.name: value_if_error
args.desc: What to show if the formula gives an error.

example.explain: Price per unit would be #DIV/0! because zero kurtas sold, so the formula shows No sales instead.

tip: IFERROR hides every error, including typos; use IFNA when you only expect a lookup to miss.

name: IFNA
purpose: Returns a value you choose only when a formula gives #N/A, such as a lookup that finds nothing.

args.name: value
args.desc: The formula to check, usually a lookup.

args.name: value_if_na
args.desc: What to show if the formula returns #N/A.

example.explain: Looks up product P105, which is missing, and shows Not in list instead of #N/A.

tip: Better than IFERROR for lookups because a real mistake such as a wrong column number still shows as an error.

name: IFS
purpose: Checks several conditions in order and returns the value for the first one that is true.

args.name: value_if_true1
args.desc: What to return if the first condition is true.

args.name: logical_test2, value_if_true2, ...
args.desc: More condition and result pairs, checked in order.

example.explain: Gives Meena grade B because 82 fails the first test but passes the second one.

tip: End with TRUE and a default value, otherwise a score that matches nothing returns #N/A.

name: IMABS
purpose: Returns the size (modulus) of a complex number.

args.name: inumber
args.desc: A complex number as text such as "3+4i".

example.explain: Finds the distance of 3+4i from zero, which is 5.

tip: Complex numbers in Excel are text, so build them with COMPLEX rather than typing them by hand.

name: IMAGE
purpose: Shows a picture from a web address inside a cell.

args.name: source
args.desc: The https web address of the picture (BMP, JPG, GIF, TIFF, PNG, ICO or WEBP).

args.name: alt_text
args.desc: A description of the picture for screen readers.

args.name: sizing
args.desc: 0 fit in cell (default), 1 fill the cell, 2 original size, 3 custom height and width.

args.name: height
args.desc: Custom height in pixels when sizing is 3.

args.name: width
args.desc: Custom width in pixels when sizing is 3.

example.result: the product photo shown inside the cell
example.explain: Loads the bottle photo from its web link into the cell; it needs Microsoft 365 and an internet connection, so the page shows the expected result instead of running it.

tip: The link must start with https and be publicly reachable; pictures on a company SharePoint behind a login will not load.

name: IMAGINARY
purpose: Returns the imaginary part of a complex number.

args.name: inumber
args.desc: A complex number as text such as "3+4i".

example.explain: Pulls out the imaginary coefficient 4 from 3+4i.

name: IMARGUMENT
purpose: Returns the angle (argument) of a complex number in radians.

example.explain: Finds the angle of 3+4i measured from the real axis, about 0.9273 radians.

tip: Wrap it in DEGREES() to see the angle in degrees.

name: IMCONJUGATE
purpose: Returns the complex conjugate of a complex number by flipping the sign of its imaginary part.

example.explain: Turns 3+4i into its conjugate 3-4i.

name: IMCOS
purpose: Returns the cosine of a complex number.

example.explain: Calculates the cosine of the complex number 1+i.

name: IMCOSH
purpose: Returns the hyperbolic cosine of a complex number.

example.explain: Calculates the hyperbolic cosine of 1+i.

name: IMCOT
purpose: Returns the cotangent of a complex number.

example.explain: Calculates the cotangent of 1+i.

name: IMCSC
purpose: Returns the cosecant of a complex number.

example.explain: Calculates the cosecant (1 divided by sine) of 1+i.

name: IMCSCH
purpose: Returns the hyperbolic cosecant of a complex number.

example.explain: Calculates the hyperbolic cosecant of 1+i.

name: IMDIV
purpose: Divides one complex number by another.

args.name: inumber2
args.desc: The complex number to divide by (denominator).

example.explain: Divides -238+240i by 10+24i to get 5+12i.

name: IMEXP
purpose: Returns e raised to the power of a complex number.

example.explain: Calculates e to the power 1+i.

name: IMLN
purpose: Returns the natural logarithm of a complex number.

example.explain: Calculates the natural log of 3+4i.

name: IMLOG10
purpose: Returns the base-10 logarithm of a complex number.

example.explain: Calculates the base-10 log of 3+4i.

name: IMLOG2
purpose: Returns the base-2 logarithm of a complex number.

example.explain: Calculates the base-2 log of 3+4i.
