name: IMPOWER
purpose: Raises a complex number to a power.

args.name: number
args.desc: The power to raise it to.

example.explain: Squares 2+3i to get -5+12i.

name: IMPRODUCT
purpose: Multiplies complex numbers together.

example.explain: Multiplies 3+4i by 5-3i to get 27+11i.

name: IMREAL
purpose: Returns the real part of a complex number.

example.explain: Pulls out the real coefficient 6 from 6-9i.

name: IMSEC
purpose: Returns the secant of a complex number.

example.explain: Calculates the secant (1 divided by cosine) of 1+i.

name: IMSECH
purpose: Returns the hyperbolic secant of a complex number.

example.explain: Calculates the hyperbolic secant of 1+i.

name: IMSIN
purpose: Returns the sine of a complex number.

example.explain: Calculates the sine of 1+i.

name: IMSINH
purpose: Returns the hyperbolic sine of a complex number.

example.explain: Calculates the hyperbolic sine of 1+i.

name: IMSQRT
purpose: Returns the square root of a complex number.

example.explain: Finds the square root of 3+4i, which is 2+i.

name: IMSUB
purpose: Subtracts one complex number from another.

args.name: inumber1
args.desc: The complex number to subtract from.

example.explain: Subtracts 5+3i from 13+4i to get 8+i.

name: IMSUM
purpose: Adds complex numbers together.

example.explain: Adds 3+4i and 5-3i to get 8+i.

tip: A normal SUM ignores complex numbers because they are text; use IMSUM.

name: IMTAN
purpose: Returns the tangent of a complex number.

example.explain: Calculates the tangent of 1+i.

name: INDEX
purpose: Returns the value at a given row and column position inside a range.

args.name: row_num
args.desc: Which row of the range to go to.

args.name: column_num
args.desc: Which column of the range to go to.

args.name: area_num
args.desc: In the reference form, which of several ranges to use.

example.explain: Goes to row 2 (Coffee) and column 3 (Jun) of the sales block and returns 110 units.

tip: Pair it with MATCH for the row and column numbers to get a lookup that survives inserted columns.

name: INDIRECT
purpose: Turns text that looks like a cell address into a real reference and returns what is there.

args.name: ref_text
args.desc: Text holding an address such as "B3" or "'Apr'!B5".

args.name: a1
args.desc: TRUE or left out for A1 style addresses, FALSE for R1C1 style.

example.explain: Reads the address B3 written in A2 and returns the amount stored in that cell.

tip: INDIRECT recalculates on every change and breaks silently when sheets are renamed, so keep it for dropdown-driven sheet names.

name: INFO
purpose: Returns information about the current Excel session, such as the calculation mode or the operating system.

example.explain: Reports whether the workbook recalculates automatically or manually; the answer depends on your own Excel settings.

tip: INFO("system") returns "mac" on a Mac and "pcdos" on Windows, useful for formulas that must work on both.

name: INT
purpose: Rounds a number down to the nearest whole number.

example.explain: Drops the paise and keeps ₹1,234 by rounding down.

tip: For negative numbers INT goes further from zero (INT(-2.5) is -3); use TRUNC to simply cut the decimals.

name: INTERCEPT
purpose: Returns the point where a straight trend line crosses the y-axis.

args.name: known_y's
args.desc: The values you want to explain, such as sales.

args.name: known_x's
args.desc: The values that drive them, such as ad spend.

example.explain: Finds the baseline sales of about ₹65,000 the trend line predicts with zero ad spend.

tip: Use it with SLOPE: predicted sales = INTERCEPT + SLOPE × ad spend.

name: INTRATE
purpose: Returns the interest rate for a fully invested security such as a T-bill or commercial paper.

args.name: basis
args.desc: Day count method: 0 US 30/360 (default), 1 actual/actual, 2 actual/360, 3 actual/365, 4 European 30/360.

example.explain: Works out the yearly interest rate earned on ₹10 lakh that grows to ₹10.18 lakh in three months, using a 365-day year.

tip: Format the result as a percentage; basis 3 (actual/365) matches how Indian money market rates are usually quoted.

name: IPMT
purpose: Returns the interest part of a loan payment for a given period.

args.name: rate
args.desc: Interest rate per period, such as annual rate divided by 12.

args.name: per
args.desc: The period you want, from 1 to nper.

args.name: fv
args.desc: Balance left after the last payment, usually 0.

args.name: type
args.desc: 0 or left out if payments are at the end of each period, 1 if at the start.

example.explain: Shows how much of the first monthly EMI on a ₹50 lakh home loan at 8.5% goes towards interest.

tip: Enter the loan as a negative number (or put a minus before PMT-style results) so the answer shows as a positive outflow.

name: IRR
purpose: Returns the yearly rate of return for a series of regular cash flows.

args.name: values
args.desc: The cash flows, starting with the investment as a negative number.

args.name: guess
args.desc: A starting guess for the rate; 10% if left out.

example.explain: Finds the return earned on a ₹5 lakh machine that brings in rising cash over four years.

tip: IRR assumes equal gaps between cash flows; for real dates such as SIP instalments use XIRR.

name: ISBLANK
purpose: Returns TRUE if a cell is completely empty.

example.explain: Flags that Asha's phone number cell is empty.

tip: A cell holding a formula that returns "" is not blank; test with B2="" to catch both cases.

name: ISERR
purpose: Returns TRUE if a value is any error except #N/A.

args.name: value
args.desc: The value or formula to check.

example.explain: Detects that dividing revenue by zero units gives an error.

tip: Use ISERR when #N/A means something useful (such as not found) and you only want to catch real calculation errors.

name: ISERROR
purpose: Returns TRUE if a value is any kind of error.

args.name: value
args.desc: The value or formula to check.

example.explain: Shows TRUE because the lookup for code P109 fails with #N/A.

tip: Inside IF, IFERROR(...) is shorter than IF(ISERROR(...),...,...).

name: ISEVEN
purpose: Returns TRUE if a number is even.

args.name: number
args.desc: The number to test; decimals are cut off first.

example.explain: Checks that invoice number 1024 is even.

tip: =ISEVEN(ROW()) inside conditional formatting shades every other row.

name: ISFORMULA
purpose: Returns TRUE if a cell contains a formula.

example.explain: Confirms the GST cell is calculated by a formula, not typed in.

tip: Use it in conditional formatting to colour hard-typed numbers in a column that should be all formulas.

name: ISLOGICAL
purpose: Returns TRUE if a value is TRUE or FALSE.

example.explain: Confirms the Paid? cell holds a real TRUE value, not the text "TRUE".

name: ISNA
purpose: Returns TRUE if a value is the #N/A error.

args.name: value
args.desc: The value or formula to check.

example.explain: Shows TRUE because Chennai is not in the branch list, so MATCH returns #N/A.

tip: =NOT(ISNA(MATCH(...))) is a quick 'is it in the list?' check.

name: ISNONTEXT
purpose: Returns TRUE if a value is not text, including empty cells.

example.explain: Returns TRUE because 45000 is a number, not text.

tip: Blank cells also return TRUE, so combine with ISBLANK if that matters.

name: ISNUMBER
purpose: Returns TRUE if a value is a number.

example.explain: Shows FALSE because 45000 was stored as text (from a bank export), which is why SUM ignores it.

tip: =ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Ltd",A2)) is the classic 'does the cell contain this word?' test.

name: ISO.CEILING
purpose: Rounds a number up to the nearest multiple, always upwards, whatever its sign.

args.name: significance
args.desc: The multiple to round to; 1 if left out.

example.explain: Rounds ₹1,234 up to the next multiple of ₹50.

tip: Works the same as CEILING.PRECISE; CEILING.MATH is the usual choice in new files.

name: ISODD
purpose: Returns TRUE if a number is odd.

args.name: number
args.desc: The number to test; decimals are cut off first.

example.explain: Checks that seat number 7 is odd.

name: ISOMITTED
purpose: Checks whether an optional argument was left out when a LAMBDA was called.

example.explain: Calls a GST LAMBDA without the rate, so ISOMITTED is TRUE and the default 18% is used.

tip: Put optional LAMBDA parameters in square brackets and give them a default with ISOMITTED.

name: ISOWEEKNUM
purpose: Returns the ISO week number of a date, where weeks start on Monday.

example.explain: Shows that 1 April 2026, the start of FY 2026-27, falls in ISO week 14.

tip: ISO week 1 is the week with the year's first Thursday, so early January dates can belong to week 52 or 53.

name: ISPMT
purpose: Returns the interest paid in a period when the loan principal is repaid in equal parts.

args.name: per
args.desc: The period to look at, counting from 0.

example.explain: Finds the interest for month 1 (after one principal repayment) on a ₹12 lakh loan repaid in 12 equal principal parts.

tip: Periods start at 0 here, unlike IPMT where they start at 1; for normal EMI loans use IPMT.

name: ISREF
purpose: Returns TRUE if a value is a cell reference.

example.explain: Confirms A2 is a valid cell reference.

tip: =ISREF(INDIRECT("'Apr'!A1")) checks whether a sheet called Apr exists.

name: ISTEXT
purpose: Returns TRUE if a value is text.

example.explain: Confirms the mobile number is stored as text, which keeps it from being shown in scientific format.

tip: Use =SUMPRODUCT(--ISTEXT(A2:A100)) to count numbers stored as text in a column.

name: JIS
purpose: Converts half-width (single-byte) characters to full-width (double-byte) characters, mainly for Japanese text.

example.explain: Converts the letters ABC to their full-width forms; it only works when an East Asian language is enabled in Office.

tip: Rarely needed outside Japanese data; ASC does the opposite conversion.

name: KURT
purpose: Measures how peaked or flat a set of values is compared with a normal distribution.

example.explain: Measures how sharply daily order counts cluster around their average.

tip: Positive kurtosis means more extreme days than a normal curve would expect; you need at least four values.

name: LAMBDA
purpose: Creates your own reusable function from a formula with named inputs.

args.name: parameter1, parameter2, ...
args.desc: Names for the inputs your function takes.

args.name: calculation
args.desc: The formula that uses those names; it is always the last argument.

example.explain: Defines a quick price-with-GST function and calls it on ₹2,500 to get ₹2,950.

tip: Save a LAMBDA under Formulas > Define Name (for example GSTINCL) to call it like a built-in function anywhere in the workbook.

name: LARGE
purpose: Returns the k-th largest value in a range, such as the second highest sale.

args.name: k
args.desc: Which position from the top: 1 for largest, 2 for second largest.

example.explain: Returns the second highest sales figure in the team.

tip: =LARGE(B2:B6,{1,2,3}) returns the top three in one go in Microsoft 365.

name: LCM
purpose: Returns the least common multiple of whole numbers.

example.explain: Finds that deliveries every 4 and every 6 days land on the same day every 12 days.

name: LEFT
purpose: Returns a set number of characters from the start of a text.

args.name: text
args.desc: The text to take characters from.

args.name: num_chars
args.desc: How many characters to take; 1 if left out.

example.explain: Pulls the two-digit state code 27 (Maharashtra) from the start of the GSTIN.

tip: LEFT always returns text, so wrap it in VALUE() if you need to do maths with the result.

name: LEFTB
purpose: Returns characters from the start of a text, counting by bytes for double-byte languages.

args.name: text
args.desc: The text to take characters from.

args.name: num_bytes
args.desc: How many bytes to take; 1 if left out.

example.explain: Takes the first three bytes of Mumbai; with English text each character is one byte, so it works like LEFT.

tip: Only differs from LEFT when a double-byte language such as Japanese, Chinese or Korean is set as the default editing language.

name: LEN
purpose: Returns the number of characters in a text, including spaces.

args.name: text
args.desc: The text or cell to measure.

example.explain: Counts the characters in the PAN, which should always be 10.

tip: =LEN(A2)<>LEN(TRIM(A2)) flags cells with stray extra spaces.

name: LENB
purpose: Returns the number of bytes used by a text, which differs from LEN only for double-byte languages.

example.explain: Counts 4 bytes in Pune because English letters use one byte each.

name: LET
purpose: Gives names to values or parts of a formula so a long formula is easier to read and faster to calculate.

args.name: name_value1
args.desc: The value or formula that name stands for.

args.name: calculation
args.desc: The final formula that uses the names; always the last argument.

example.explain: Names the taxable value and the GST amount, then adds them to get the invoice total.

tip: Names cannot look like cell addresses, so use gst_amt rather than GST1.

name: LINEST
purpose: Returns the slope and intercept (and optional statistics) of the best-fit straight line for your data.

args.name: known_y's
args.desc: The values you want to explain.

args.name: const
args.desc: TRUE or left out to calculate the intercept, FALSE to force it to zero.

args.name: stats
args.desc: TRUE to also return R squared, standard errors and more.

example.explain: Spills the slope (₹8,900 extra sales per ₹1,000 of ads) and the intercept (₹65,000) side by side.

tip: With several x columns LINEST does multiple regression, but it returns the slopes in reverse column order.

name: LN
purpose: Returns the natural logarithm (base e) of a number.

example.explain: Finds the continuously compounded growth needed to double money.

tip: =LN(2)/rate gives the doubling time for continuous growth; the Rule of 72 is the quick mental version.

name: LOG
purpose: Returns the logarithm of a number to the base you choose.

args.name: base
args.desc: The base of the logarithm; 10 if left out.

example.explain: Works out that money growing at 12% a year doubles in about 6.12 years.

tip: NPER gives the same answer for investments and also handles regular SIP instalments.

name: LOG10
purpose: Returns the base-10 logarithm of a number.

example.explain: Shows that ₹1 crore is 10 to the power 7, that is, it has 8 digits.

name: LOGEST
purpose: Fits an exponential growth curve to your data and returns its growth factor and starting value.

args.name: known_y's
args.desc: The values that grow, such as monthly subscribers.

args.name: const
args.desc: TRUE or left out to calculate the starting value, FALSE to force it to 1.

args.name: stats
args.desc: TRUE to also return regression statistics.

example.explain: Shows subscribers grow by a factor of 1.1 (10%) a month, starting from about 90.9 at month zero.

tip: Subtract 1 from the growth factor to read it as a monthly growth rate.

name: LOGINV
purpose: Older version of LOGNORM.INV that returns the value for a given lognormal probability.

example.explain: Finds the value whose cumulative lognormal probability is 0.039084.

tip: Kept for old files; use LOGNORM.INV in new work.

name: LOGNORM.DIST
purpose: Returns the lognormal distribution, used for values like prices that cannot go below zero.

args.name: cumulative
args.desc: TRUE for the cumulative probability, FALSE for the density.

example.explain: Gives the probability that a lognormal value with these settings is 4 or less.

name: LOGNORM.INV
purpose: Returns the value for a given probability in a lognormal distribution.

example.explain: Works backwards from a probability of 0.039084 to the value 4.

name: LOGNORMDIST
purpose: Older version of LOGNORM.DIST that returns the cumulative lognormal probability.

example.explain: Gives the probability that the value is 4 or less.

tip: Kept for old files; use LOGNORM.DIST, which can also return the density.

name: LOOKUP
purpose: Finds a value in one row or column and returns the matching item from another row or column.

args.name: lookup_vector
args.desc: The single row or column to search, sorted smallest to largest.

args.name: result_vector
args.desc: The row or column to return from, the same size as lookup_vector.

example.explain: Finds the slab for ₹1,80,000 in sales (₹1 lakh and above) and returns the 3% commission rate.

tip: LOOKUP always does an approximate match on sorted data; for exact matches use XLOOKUP or VLOOKUP with FALSE.

name: LOWER
purpose: Converts all letters in a text to lowercase.

example.explain: Tidies an email address typed in mixed case into all lowercase.

tip: Use LOWER(TRIM(A2)) before comparing or de-duplicating email lists.

name: MAKEARRAY
purpose: Builds an array of a chosen size by running a LAMBDA for every row and column position.

args.name: lambda
args.desc: A LAMBDA with two inputs, the row number and the column number, that returns each value.

example.explain: Builds a 3 by 3 rate card where each cell is the base rate times the row number times the column number.

tip: The LAMBDA must take exactly two parameters, even if you only use one of them.

name: MAP
purpose: Runs a LAMBDA on each value of one or more arrays and returns the results in the same shape.

args.name: array1
args.desc: The first array whose values are passed in.

args.name: array2, ...
args.desc: More arrays of the same size, passed in alongside.

args.name: lambda
args.desc: A LAMBDA with one input per array; always the last argument.

example.explain: Gives a 10% discount only on orders above ₹2,000 and leaves the rest unchanged.

tip: Use MAP when IF or AND would otherwise collapse a whole range into one answer.

name: MATCH
purpose: Returns the position of a value within a row or column.

args.name: lookup_array
args.desc: The single row or column to search.

args.name: match_type
args.desc: 0 for exact match; 1 or left out for largest value less than or equal (sorted ascending); -1 for smallest value greater than or equal (sorted descending).

example.explain: Finds Pune in the third position of the branch list.

tip: The default match type is 1, not exact, so always type 0 unless your list is sorted bands.

name: MAX
purpose: Returns the largest number in a set of values.

example.explain: Finds the highest sales figure in the team.

tip: =MAX(0,A2-B2) is a neat way to stop a shortfall from going negative.

name: MAXA
purpose: Returns the largest value in a list, counting TRUE as 1 and text or FALSE as 0.

example.explain: Counts the TRUE entry as 1, which is larger than 0.6 and 0.8.

tip: Use plain MAX unless you really want logical values to count.

name: MAXIFS
purpose: Returns the largest value among cells that meet one or more conditions.

args.name: max_range
args.desc: The cells to find the maximum in.

args.name: criteria_range1
args.desc: The cells to test with the first condition.

args.name: criteria1
args.desc: The first condition, such as "North" or ">100000".

example.explain: Finds the best sales figure in the North region.

tip: Put the condition in a cell and refer to it, for example A9, instead of typing "North" into the formula.

name: MDETERM
purpose: Returns the determinant of a square matrix.

args.name: array
args.desc: A square range of numbers, with the same number of rows and columns.

example.explain: Calculates 2×4 minus 3×1 for the 2 by 2 matrix.

tip: A determinant of 0 means the matrix has no inverse, so MINVERSE will return #NUM!.

name: MDURATION
purpose: Returns the modified duration of a bond, showing how much its price moves when yields change.

example.explain: Estimates the percentage price change of a 5-year 7.5% bond for each 1% move in yields.

tip: A modified duration of 4 means roughly a 4% fall in price if yields rise by 1%.

name: MEDIAN
purpose: Returns the middle value of a set of numbers.

example.explain: Finds the middle salary, which is not pulled up or down by one very high or low pay.

tip: Prefer MEDIAN to AVERAGE for salaries and property prices, where a few big numbers distort the mean.

name: MID
purpose: Returns a set number of characters from the middle of a text, starting at a position you choose.

args.name: text
args.desc: The text to take characters from.

args.name: start_num
args.desc: Position of the first character to take, counting from 1.

example.explain: Extracts the 10-character PAN that sits inside the GSTIN from position 3.

tip: MID returns text, so wrap it in VALUE() when the piece you pull out is a number.

name: MIDB
purpose: Returns characters from the middle of a text, counting by bytes for double-byte languages.

args.name: text
args.desc: The text to take characters from.

example.explain: Takes the first three bytes of Chennai; with English text it behaves just like MID.

name: MIN
purpose: Returns the smallest number in a set of values.

example.explain: Finds the lowest sales figure in the team.

tip: =MIN(B2*10%,5000) caps a 10% incentive at ₹5,000.

name: MINA
purpose: Returns the smallest value in a list, counting FALSE and text as 0 and TRUE as 1.

example.explain: Counts the FALSE entry as 0, so the minimum is 0 rather than 8.

tip: Use plain MIN unless you want logical values and text to count.

name: MINIFS
purpose: Returns the smallest value among cells that meet one or more conditions.

args.name: min_range
args.desc: The cells to find the minimum in.

args.name: criteria_range1
args.desc: The cells to test with the first condition.

example.explain: Finds the lowest sales figure in the South region.

tip: If no cell meets the condition MINIFS returns 0, not an error, so check with COUNTIFS first.

name: MINUTE
purpose: Returns the minutes (0 to 59) from a time.

args.name: serial_number
args.desc: The time to read the minutes from.

example.explain: Reads the minutes part of the 2:45 pm login time.

tip: To get total minutes from a duration use =A2*1440 instead.

name: MINVERSE
purpose: Returns the inverse of a square matrix.

example.explain: Spills the 2 by 2 inverse of the matrix, used for solving simultaneous equations.

tip: =MMULT(MINVERSE(A),B) solves a set of linear equations in one formula.

name: MIRR
purpose: Returns the rate of return of cash flows using separate rates for borrowing and for reinvesting.

args.name: values
args.desc: The cash flows, with at least one negative and one positive.

args.name: finance_rate
args.desc: Interest rate paid on money borrowed for the investment.

args.name: reinvest_rate
args.desc: Rate earned when the cash received is reinvested.

example.explain: Calculates the return on the ₹5 lakh project assuming a 10% loan cost and 12% earned on reinvested cash.

tip: MIRR is more realistic than IRR when cash flows cannot really be reinvested at the IRR itself.

name: MMULT
purpose: Returns the matrix product of two arrays.

args.name: array1
args.desc: The first matrix; its number of columns must equal the rows of array2.

example.explain: Multiplies each branch's quantities by the item rates and adds them, giving each branch's total sales.

tip: Mismatched sizes give #VALUE!; check that columns of the first equal rows of the second.

name: MOD
purpose: Returns the remainder after one number is divided by another.

example.explain: Finds the 5 months left over after 2 full years of service in a 29-month tenure.

tip: =MOD(end-start,1) gives the right shift length even when a night shift crosses midnight.

name: MODE
purpose: Older version of MODE.SNGL that returns the most frequent number in a list.

example.explain: Finds the shoe size that sells most often.

tip: Kept for old files; use MODE.SNGL, or MODE.MULT when there may be a tie.

name: MODE.MULT
purpose: Returns every value that appears most often in a list, as a vertical array.

example.explain: Spills both sizes 8 and 9 because each sold twice.

tip: If no value repeats MODE.MULT returns #N/A.

name: MODE.SNGL
purpose: Returns the value that appears most often in a list of numbers.

args.name: number1
args.desc: The first number, cell or range to check.

args.name: number2, ...
args.desc: More numbers or ranges, up to 254.

example.explain: Finds the most common delay across five deliveries, which is 2 days.

tip: If no value repeats you get #N/A; wrap it in IFERROR to show a friendly message.

name: MONTH
purpose: Returns the month number (1 to 12) from a date.

args.name: serial_number
args.desc: The date you want the month from.

example.explain: Pulls the month number out of an invoice dated 15 August 2026.

tip: For an Indian FY month number (April = 1) use =MOD(MONTH(A2)-4,12)+1.

name: MROUND
purpose: Rounds a number to the nearest multiple you choose.

args.name: multiple
args.desc: The multiple to round to, such as 5 or 0.05.

example.explain: Rounds a price of 1,247 to the nearest 5 rupees, giving 1,245.

tip: Number and multiple must have the same sign, otherwise MROUND returns #NUM!.

name: MULTINOMIAL
purpose: Returns the ratio of the factorial of a sum to the product of the factorials of its parts.

example.explain: Counts the ways to split 9 people into teams of 2, 3 and 4.

name: MUNIT
purpose: Returns an identity matrix of the size you ask for.

args.name: dimension
args.desc: The number of rows and columns of the square matrix.

example.explain: Spills a 3 by 3 identity matrix with 1s on the diagonal.

name: N
purpose: Converts a value to a number, turning text into 0.

example.explain: Treats the text Pending as 0 and adds the 2,500, giving 2,500.

tip: Handy for adding a hidden comment inside a formula: =A2*1.18+N("GST at 18%").

name: NA
purpose: Returns the #N/A error on purpose, meaning a value is not available.

example.explain: Shows #N/A when the amount is blank so charts skip the point instead of plotting zero.

tip: Line charts leave a gap for #N/A but drop to zero for a blank or 0.

name: NEGBINOM.DIST
purpose: Returns the negative binomial probability of a number of failures before a set number of successes.

args.name: probability_s
args.desc: The chance of success on each try.

args.name: cumulative
args.desc: TRUE for the running total probability, FALSE for the exact probability.

example.explain: Probability of at most 10 unanswered calls before 5 sales when each call converts 25% of the time.

name: NEGBINOMDIST
purpose: Returns the negative binomial probability (older version kept for compatibility).

args.name: probability_s
args.desc: The chance of success on each try.

example.explain: Probability of exactly 10 failed calls before the 5th sale at a 25% conversion rate.

tip: Use NEGBINOM.DIST instead; it also gives the cumulative probability.

name: NETWORKDAYS
purpose: Counts working days between two dates, skipping Saturdays, Sundays and listed holidays.

args.name: start_date
args.desc: The first date, counted if it is a working day.

args.name: holidays
args.desc: A range of holiday dates to skip.

example.explain: Counts working days in October 2026 after removing weekends, Gandhi Jayanti and Dussehra.

tip: Keep holidays in a named range or Table so every formula uses the same list.

name: NETWORKDAYS.INTL
purpose: Counts working days between two dates with weekends you define and holidays skipped.

args.name: weekend
args.desc: A code such as 11 for Sunday only, or a 7 digit text like "0000011" (Monday first, 1 = off).

args.name: holidays
args.desc: A range of holiday dates to skip.

example.explain: Counts October 2026 working days for a shop that works six days a week and closes only on Sundays.

tip: For alternate Saturdays off, calculate in two parts or use a helper list of off days as holidays.

name: NOMINAL
purpose: Converts an effective annual interest rate into the nominal annual rate.

args.name: npery
args.desc: How many times a year interest is compounded.

example.explain: Finds the quoted annual rate that gives an effective 8.25% with monthly compounding.

tip: EFFECT does the reverse conversion.

name: NORM.DIST
purpose: Returns the normal distribution value for a given mean and standard deviation.

args.name: cumulative
args.desc: TRUE for the probability of being at or below x, FALSE for the height of the curve.

example.explain: Shows that about 93% of candidates score 80 or less when marks average 65 with a spread of 10.

name: NORM.INV
purpose: Returns the value below which a given share of a normal distribution falls.

example.explain: Finds the cut-off score for the top 10% when marks average 65 with a spread of 10.

name: NORM.S.DIST
purpose: Returns the standard normal distribution value (mean 0, standard deviation 1).

args.name: cumulative
args.desc: TRUE for the cumulative probability, FALSE for the curve height.

example.explain: Probability that a value is less than one standard deviation above the mean.

name: NORM.S.INV
purpose: Returns the z-score for a given cumulative probability in the standard normal distribution.

example.explain: Gives the z-score used for a one-sided 95% confidence level.

name: NORMDIST
purpose: Returns the normal distribution value (older version kept for compatibility).

args.name: cumulative
args.desc: TRUE for cumulative, FALSE for the curve height.

example.explain: Probability of a score at or below 80 when the mean is 65 and spread is 10.

tip: Use NORM.DIST instead in new workbooks.

name: NORMINV
purpose: Returns the inverse of the normal cumulative distribution (older version kept for compatibility).

example.explain: Finds the score that 90% of candidates fall below.

tip: Use NORM.INV instead in new workbooks.

name: NORMSDIST
purpose: Returns the standard normal cumulative distribution (older version kept for compatibility).

example.explain: Probability that a standard normal value is below 1.

tip: Use NORM.S.DIST(z,TRUE) instead.

name: NORMSINV
purpose: Returns the inverse of the standard normal distribution (older version kept for compatibility).

example.explain: Returns the z-score for 95% cumulative probability.

tip: Use NORM.S.INV instead.

name: NOT
purpose: Reverses a logical value, turning TRUE into FALSE and FALSE into TRUE.

example.explain: Checks whether an invoice is still unpaid; it is paid, so the answer is FALSE.

tip: A2<>"Paid" does the same job and is often easier to read.

name: NOW
purpose: Returns the current date and time, updating whenever the sheet recalculates.

example.explain: Shows the date and time right now; the value changes every time the sheet recalculates.

tip: To stamp a fixed time instead, press ⌘ + ; then ⌘ + Shift + ; in the cell.

name: NPER
purpose: Returns the number of periods needed for a loan or investment.

args.name: rate
args.desc: Interest rate per period, e.g. annual rate divided by 12.

args.name: pmt
args.desc: Payment each period; money you pay out is negative.

args.name: pv
args.desc: Present value or amount you start with.

args.name: fv
args.desc: Target value at the end; 0 if left out.

args.name: type
args.desc: 1 if payments are at the start of each period, 0 or blank for the end.

example.explain: Works out how many months a 15,000 rupee SIP at 12% a year needs to reach 10 lakh.

tip: Keep the signs consistent: money going out is negative, money coming back is positive.

name: NPV
purpose: Returns the net present value of future cash flows at a given discount rate.

args.name: value1
args.desc: The first future cash flow, received at the end of period 1.

args.name: value2, ...
args.desc: More cash flows in time order.

example.explain: Discounts three years of inflows at 10% and subtracts the 6 lakh spent today, giving a positive NPV of about 13,824 rupees.

tip: NPV assumes the first value comes after one period, so subtract today's investment outside the function.

name: NUMBERVALUE
purpose: Converts text to a number using the decimal and group separators you specify.

args.name: decimal_separator
args.desc: The character used as the decimal point in the text.

args.name: group_separator
args.desc: The character used to group thousands in the text.

example.explain: Turns an amount exported in European style (dots for groups, comma for decimals) into the number 125000.5.

tip: Useful for bank or vendor exports from other countries where VALUE gives #VALUE!.

name: OCT2BIN
purpose: Converts an octal number to binary.

args.name: places
args.desc: How many characters to show, padding with zeros.

example.explain: Converts octal 7 to binary and pads it to four digits.

name: OCT2DEC
purpose: Converts an octal number to decimal.

example.explain: Converts octal 144 to its decimal value.

name: OCT2HEX
purpose: Converts an octal number to hexadecimal.

args.name: places
args.desc: How many characters to show, padding with zeros.

example.explain: Converts octal 144 to hexadecimal.

name: ODD
purpose: Rounds a number up to the nearest odd whole number.

example.explain: Rounds 22 up to the next odd number, 23.

name: ODDFPRICE
purpose: Returns the price per 100 face value of a bond with an odd (short or long) first period.
syntax: ODDFPRICE(settlement, maturity, issue, first_coupon, rate, yld, redemption, frequency, [basis])

example.explain: Prices a 7.85% bond with a long first coupon period when the market yield is 6.25%.

name: ODDFYIELD
purpose: Returns the yield of a bond with an odd first period.
syntax: ODDFYIELD(settlement, maturity, issue, first_coupon, rate, pr, redemption, frequency, [basis])

example.explain: Finds the annual yield of the same odd-first-period bond bought at 113.60.

name: ODDLPRICE
purpose: Returns the price per 100 face value of a bond with an odd last period.
syntax: ODDLPRICE(settlement, maturity, last_interest, rate, yld, redemption, frequency, [basis])

example.explain: Prices a 3.75% bond whose final period is shorter than usual at a 4.05% yield.

name: ODDLYIELD
purpose: Returns the yield of a bond with an odd last period.
syntax: ODDLYIELD(settlement, maturity, last_interest, rate, pr, redemption, frequency, [basis])

example.explain: Finds the yield of a bond with a short final period bought at 99.875.

name: OFFSET
purpose: Returns a range that is a set number of rows and columns away from a starting cell, with the size you choose.

args.name: rows
args.desc: How many rows to move down (negative moves up).

args.name: cols
args.desc: How many columns to move right (negative moves left).

args.name: height
args.desc: How many rows tall the result should be.

args.name: width
args.desc: How many columns wide the result should be.

example.explain: Starts at B2, moves down 2 rows to June and takes a block 3 rows tall, adding June to August sales.

tip: For a rolling last-3-months total use COUNT for the rows argument: =SUM(OFFSET(B2,COUNT(B2:B6)-3,0,3,1)).

name: OR
purpose: Returns TRUE if at least one of the conditions is TRUE.

example.explain: Passes a trainee who has either 75% attendance or a score of 80, and this one scored 82.

tip: Inside IF, OR lets you replace several nested IFs: =IF(OR(...),"Yes","No").

name: PDURATION
purpose: Returns how many periods an investment needs to grow to a target value.

args.name: fv
args.desc: The value you want to reach.

example.explain: Shows how many years a 5 lakh FD at 7% a year takes to double to 10 lakh.

tip: Quick check: the Rule of 72 says 72 / 7 is about 10.3 years.

name: PEARSON
purpose: Returns the Pearson correlation coefficient between two sets of numbers.

args.name: array2
args.desc: The second set, the same size as the first.

example.explain: Measures how closely monthly sales move with ad spend; close to 1 means a strong positive link.

tip: PEARSON gives the same answer as CORREL.

name: PERCENTILE
purpose: Returns the value at a given percentile of a range (older version kept for compatibility).

args.name: k
args.desc: The percentile as a decimal from 0 to 1.

example.explain: Finds the salary below which 90% of the team falls.

tip: Use PERCENTILE.INC instead; it works the same way.

name: PERCENTILE.EXC
purpose: Returns the k-th percentile of a range, where k is between 0 and 1 exclusive.

args.name: k
args.desc: The percentile, greater than 0 and less than 1.

example.explain: Finds the 25th percentile salary using the exclusive method.

tip: For small lists, extreme k values like 0.05 return #NUM! with the .EXC version.

name: PERCENTILE.INC
purpose: Returns the k-th percentile of a range, where k is between 0 and 1 inclusive.

args.name: k
args.desc: The percentile as a decimal from 0 to 1.

example.explain: Finds the salary at the 90th percentile, a common benchmark for top-band pay.

tip: Write k as a decimal (0.9), not 90.

name: PERCENTOF
purpose: Returns what share a subset of values is of the total.

args.name: data_subset
args.desc: The values that make up the part.

args.name: data_all
args.desc: All the values that make up the total.

example.explain: Shows that North brings in half of total sales.

tip: Pass PERCENTOF as the function in GROUPBY or PIVOTBY to show each group as a share of the total.

name: PERCENTRANK
purpose: Returns the rank of a value as a percentage of the range (older version kept for compatibility).

args.name: significance
args.desc: Number of significant digits, 3 if left out.

example.explain: Shows that a 48,000 salary sits exactly in the middle of the team.

tip: Use PERCENTRANK.INC instead.

name: PERCENTRANK.EXC
purpose: Returns the rank of a value as a percentage of the range, excluding 0 and 1.

args.name: significance
args.desc: Number of significant digits, 3 if left out.

example.explain: Ranks a 48,000 salary using the exclusive method.

name: PERCENTRANK.INC
purpose: Returns the rank of a value as a percentage of the range, from 0 to 1 inclusive.

args.name: significance
args.desc: Number of significant digits, 3 if left out.

example.explain: Shows that a 55,000 salary is higher than 75% of the team.

tip: Format the cell as a percentage to read it as 75%.

name: PERMUT
purpose: Returns the number of ordered arrangements of items chosen from a group.

args.name: number_chosen
args.desc: How many are picked for each arrangement.

example.explain: Counts the ways to pick a lead, deputy and note-taker from 5 team members.

tip: Use COMBIN when order does not matter.

name: PERMUTATIONA
purpose: Returns the number of ordered arrangements when items can repeat.

args.name: number_chosen
args.desc: How many are picked, repeats allowed.

example.explain: Counts every possible 4 digit ATM PIN.

name: PHI
purpose: Returns the height of the standard normal curve at a value.

example.explain: Gives the density of the standard normal curve at z = 0.75.

name: PHONETIC
purpose: Extracts the phonetic (furigana) reading from Japanese text.

args.name: reference
args.desc: The cell or range holding the Japanese text.

example.explain: Reads the furigana stored with the Japanese text; without a Japanese editing language and furigana typed through a Japanese input method, Excel returns #N/A, otherwise it returns the reading such as トウキョウ.

tip: Only useful when furigana was typed with a Japanese input method.

name: PI
purpose: Returns the value of pi, 3.14159265358979.

example.explain: Calculates the area of a circular lawn with a 7 metre radius.

name: PIVOTBY
purpose: Builds a pivot-style summary with row groups, column groups and an aggregation, all from one formula.

args.name: row_fields
args.desc: The column(s) to group down the rows.

args.name: col_fields
args.desc: The column(s) to group across the top.

args.name: function
args.desc: How to summarise, such as SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT or PERCENTOF.

args.name: field_headers
args.desc: Whether the ranges have headers and whether to show them (0 to 3).

args.name: row_total_depth
args.desc: Whether to show row totals and subtotals.

args.name: row_sort_order
args.desc: Which column to sort rows by; negative for descending.

args.name: col_total_depth
args.desc: Whether to show column totals and subtotals.

args.name: col_sort_order
args.desc: Which row to sort columns by; negative for descending.

args.name: filter_array
args.desc: TRUE/FALSE values that keep or drop rows before summarising.

args.name: relative_to
args.desc: What PERCENTOF compares against: column totals, row totals, grand total and so on.

example.explain: Spills a region by quarter sales table with row and column totals, which refreshes as soon as the data changes.

tip: Unlike a PivotTable, PIVOTBY never needs a refresh, but it cannot be formatted with pivot styles.

name: PMT
purpose: Returns the fixed payment per period for a loan, such as a monthly EMI.

args.name: rate
args.desc: Interest rate per period; divide an annual rate by 12 for monthly EMIs.

args.name: nper
args.desc: Total number of payments, e.g. years x 12.

args.name: fv
args.desc: Balance left after the last payment; 0 if left out.

args.name: type
args.desc: 1 if paid at the start of each period, 0 or blank for the end.

example.explain: Calculates the monthly EMI on a 50 lakh home loan at 8.5% for 20 years.

tip: Put a minus before the loan amount to get a positive EMI; mixing yearly rate with monthly periods is the most common mistake.

name: POISSON
purpose: Returns the Poisson distribution (older version kept for compatibility).

args.name: mean
args.desc: The average number of events expected.

args.name: cumulative
args.desc: TRUE for at most x events, FALSE for exactly x.

example.explain: Probability of exactly 3 walk-in customers in an hour when the average is 5.

tip: Use POISSON.DIST instead.

name: POISSON.DIST
purpose: Returns the Poisson probability of a number of events in a fixed period.

args.name: mean
args.desc: The average number of events expected.

args.name: cumulative
args.desc: TRUE for at most x events, FALSE for exactly x.

example.explain: Probability that a support desk gets exactly 3 calls in an hour when it averages 5.

tip: Use TRUE to plan staffing: the chance of at most x calls.

name: POWER
purpose: Raises a number to a power.

args.name: power
args.desc: The exponent to raise it to.

example.explain: Grows 1 lakh at 8% compound interest for 5 years.

tip: The ^ operator does the same: =A2*(1+B2)^C2.

name: PPMT
purpose: Returns the principal part of a loan payment for a given period.

args.name: per
args.desc: The period you want, from 1 to nper.

args.name: fv
args.desc: Balance after the last payment; 0 if left out.

args.name: type
args.desc: 1 for payments at the start of the period.

example.explain: Shows how much of the first EMI on a 50 lakh home loan actually reduces the principal.

tip: PPMT + IPMT for any month always equals the PMT amount.

name: PRICE
purpose: Returns the price per 100 face value of a bond that pays periodic interest.
syntax: PRICE(settlement, maturity, rate, yld, redemption, frequency, [basis])

example.explain: Prices a 5.75% semi-annual bond when the market yield is 6.5%.

tip: When yield is above the coupon, the price falls below 100.

name: PRICEDISC
purpose: Returns the price per 100 face value of a discounted security such as a T-bill.

example.explain: Prices a short discounted security maturing in about two weeks.

name: PRICEMAT
purpose: Returns the price per 100 face value of a security that pays interest at maturity.

example.explain: Prices a security that pays all its interest on maturity.

name: PROB
purpose: Returns the probability that values fall between two limits.

args.name: prob_range
args.desc: The probability of each outcome; must add up to 1.

args.name: upper_limit
args.desc: The upper value; if left out, PROB checks only the lower value.

example.explain: Probability that a stall sells between 1 and 3 units in a day.

name: PRODUCT
purpose: Multiplies all the numbers you give it.

example.explain: Multiplies quantity, rate and 1.18 to get the invoice value including 18% GST.

tip: PRODUCT ignores blank cells, while =A2*B2 treats a blank as 0.

name: PROPER
purpose: Capitalises the first letter of each word and lowercases the rest.

example.explain: Fixes a name typed in random case.

tip: Watch out for names like McDonald or abbreviations like GST, which PROPER changes to Mcdonald and Gst.

name: PV
purpose: Returns the present value of a series of future payments.

args.name: fv
args.desc: A lump sum at the end; 0 if left out.

args.name: type
args.desc: 1 for payments at the start of each period.

example.explain: Finds how much you need today to pay out 10,000 rupees a month for 5 years at 9%.

tip: Also tells you the maximum loan you can take for an EMI you can afford.

name: PY
purpose: Runs Python code inside a cell using Python in Excel.

args.name: python_code
args.desc: The Python code to run, typed into the cell after choosing Python mode; must be static text.

args.name: return_type
args.desc: 0 to return an Excel value, 1 to return a Python object; must be a static 0 or 1.

example.explain: Python reads the table with xl() and adds up the Sales column; it needs Microsoft 365 with Python in Excel and runs in Microsoft's cloud.

tip: You normally type =PY and press Tab (or use Formulas > Insert Python) and then write plain Python; Excel builds the PY formula for you.

name: QUARTILE
purpose: Returns a quartile of a set of numbers (older version kept for compatibility).

args.name: quart
args.desc: 0 = minimum, 1 = first quartile, 2 = median, 3 = third quartile, 4 = maximum.

example.explain: Finds the salary marking the bottom quarter of the team.

tip: Use QUARTILE.INC instead; it gives the same result.

name: QUARTILE.EXC
purpose: Returns a quartile of a set of numbers using the exclusive method.

args.name: quart
args.desc: 1, 2 or 3 for the first quartile, median or third quartile.

example.explain: Finds the first quartile salary using the exclusive method, which gives a wider spread on small lists.

tip: Box-and-whisker charts in Excel can use either method; match the one your formulas use.

name: QUARTILE.INC
purpose: Returns a quartile of a set of numbers using the inclusive method.

args.name: quart
args.desc: 0 = minimum, 1 = first quartile, 2 = median, 3 = third quartile, 4 = maximum.

example.explain: Finds the salary that marks the top quarter of the team.

tip: QUARTILE.INC(range,2) is the same as MEDIAN(range).

name: QUOTIENT
purpose: Returns the whole number part of a division, dropping the remainder.

example.explain: Counts how many full cartons of 24 you can pack from 1,250 units.

tip: Pair it with MOD to get the loose units left over.

name: RADIANS
purpose: Converts degrees to radians.

example.explain: Converts 45 degrees to radians for use in SIN, COS or TAN.

tip: Excel's trig functions expect radians, so wrap degrees in RADIANS first.

name: RAND
purpose: Returns a random decimal number from 0 up to (but not including) 1.

example.explain: Returns a new random decimal every time the sheet recalculates, so your value will differ.

tip: To freeze random values, copy and use Paste Special > Values (⌘ + Control + V).

name: RANDARRAY
purpose: Returns an array of random numbers with the size and range you choose.

args.name: whole_number
args.desc: TRUE for whole numbers, FALSE or blank for decimals.

example.explain: Spills five random 4 digit order numbers for practice data; they change on every recalculation.

tip: Combine with SORTBY to shuffle a list: =SORTBY(A2:A20,RANDARRAY(ROWS(A2:A20))).

name: RANDBETWEEN
purpose: Returns a random whole number between two numbers you choose.

example.result: a random whole number between 1000 and 9999
example.explain: Generates a random 4 digit number, such as a sample OTP, which changes on every recalculation.

tip: Great for dummy sales data: =RANDBETWEEN(50000,150000).

name: RANK
purpose: Returns the rank of a number in a list (older version kept for compatibility).

args.name: order
args.desc: 0 or blank ranks highest as 1; any other number ranks lowest as 1.

example.explain: Ranks Ravi's sales in the team; he ties with Imran for third.

tip: Use RANK.EQ instead; it behaves the same way.

name: RANK.AVG
purpose: Returns the rank of a number, giving tied values the average of their ranks.

args.name: order
args.desc: 0 or blank ranks highest as 1; any other number ranks lowest as 1.

example.explain: Ravi and Imran share 3rd and 4th place, so each gets the average rank 3.5.

name: RANK.EQ
purpose: Returns the rank of a number in a list, giving tied values the same top rank.

args.name: ref
args.desc: The list of values; lock it with $ before copying down.

args.name: order
args.desc: 0 or blank ranks highest as 1; any other number ranks lowest as 1.

example.explain: Ranks Ravi third in the sales leaderboard; Imran, with the same sales, also gets 3.

tip: Lock the list with $B$2:$B$6 (⌘ + T toggles the $ signs) before filling down.

name: RATE
purpose: Returns the interest rate per period of a loan or investment.

args.name: pmt
args.desc: Payment each period; money paid out is negative.

args.name: fv
args.desc: Value at the end; 0 if left out.

args.name: type
args.desc: 1 for payments at the start of the period.

args.name: guess
args.desc: Your guess for the rate; 10% if left out.

example.explain: Works out the real annual interest rate hidden in a car loan offer of 12,500 a month for 5 years.

tip: RATE gives the rate per period, so multiply by 12 for an annual rate on monthly EMIs.

name: RECEIVED
purpose: Returns the amount received at maturity for a fully invested discounted security.

example.explain: Calculates what 10 lakh invested in a 3 month discounted security pays back at maturity.

name: REDUCE
purpose: Runs a LAMBDA over every value in an array and returns one final accumulated result.

args.name: initial_value
args.desc: The starting value of the accumulator.

args.name: lambda
args.desc: A LAMBDA with two parameters: the running total and the current value.

example.explain: Adds up only the branches that sold more than 1 lakh.

tip: Use SCAN with the same LAMBDA to see each step of the running total.

name: REGEXEXTRACT
purpose: Extracts the part of a text that matches a regular expression pattern.

args.name: return_mode
args.desc: 0 = first match, 1 = all matches, 2 = capture groups of the first match.

example.explain: Pulls a 10 digit Indian mobile number out of a free-text note.

tip: Return mode 1 spills every match, handy for notes with two phone numbers.

name: REGEXREPLACE
purpose: Replaces the parts of a text that match a regular expression.

args.name: replacement
args.desc: The text to put in place of each match.

args.name: occurrence
args.desc: Which match to replace; 0 or blank replaces all.

example.explain: Masks the four digits of a PAN before sharing a report.

tip: Use \s+ as the pattern with " " as the replacement to squeeze any run of spaces or tabs.

name: REGEXTEST
purpose: Checks whether a text matches a regular expression and returns TRUE or FALSE.

example.explain: Confirms the PAN has five letters, four digits and a final letter.

tip: Use it in Data Validation (Custom) to block wrongly typed PANs or GSTINs.

name: REGISTER.ID
purpose: Returns the register ID of a procedure in a Windows DLL that has been registered.

args.name: procedure
args.desc: The name of the function in the DLL.

args.name: type_text
args.desc: Text describing the return and argument types.

example.explain: Registers a Windows system function and returns its ID; this only works in Excel for Windows with macro security allowing it.

tip: Not available on a Mac; use VBA or Office Scripts instead.

name: REPLACE
purpose: Replaces a set number of characters at a given position in text.

args.name: start_num
args.desc: Position of the first character to replace.

example.explain: Masks the middle six digits of a mobile number.

tip: Use SUBSTITUTE when you know the text to swap but not its position.

name: REPLACEB
purpose: Replaces part of a text based on a number of bytes, for double-byte languages.

example.explain: With English text each character is one byte, so it works just like REPLACE.

tip: Counts bytes only when a double-byte language (Chinese, Japanese, Korean) is set as default; otherwise use REPLACE.

name: REPT
purpose: Repeats text a given number of times.

args.name: number_times
args.desc: How many times to repeat it.

example.explain: Shows a 4 star customer rating as stars.

tip: =REPT("|",B2/10000) makes a quick in-cell bar chart.

name: RIGHT
purpose: Returns a set number of characters from the end of a text.

args.name: text
args.desc: The text to take characters from.

args.name: num_chars
args.desc: How many characters to return; 1 if left out.

example.explain: Picks the last three characters of a GSTIN: entity number, Z and the check digit.

tip: RIGHT always returns text; wrap it in VALUE if you need a number.

name: RIGHTB
purpose: Returns characters from the end of a text based on a number of bytes.

args.name: text
args.desc: The text to take characters from.

example.explain: With English text each character is one byte, so it returns the last four characters.

tip: Use RIGHT unless you work with double-byte languages.

name: ROMAN
purpose: Converts a number into Roman numerals as text.

example.explain: Writes the year 2026 in Roman numerals for a report cover.

tip: ARABIC converts Roman numerals back into numbers.

name: ROUND
purpose: Rounds a number to the number of digits you choose.

args.name: num_digits
args.desc: Decimal places to keep; 0 for whole numbers, negative to round to tens, hundreds and so on.

example.explain: Rounds GST of 1,525.50 to the nearest rupee.

tip: Formatting only hides decimals; ROUND changes the stored value so totals add up.

name: ROUNDDOWN
purpose: Rounds a number down, towards zero.

args.name: num_digits
args.desc: Decimal places to keep; negative rounds to tens, hundreds and so on.

example.explain: Rounds a bonus down to the lower hundred rupees.

tip: ROUNDDOWN(x,0) and TRUNC(x) give the same result.

name: ROUNDUP
purpose: Rounds a number up, away from zero.

args.name: num_digits
args.desc: Decimal places to keep; 0 for whole numbers.

example.explain: Works out that 23 staff need 6 cabs of 4 seats each.

tip: Use it whenever a part unit still needs a whole one: cabs, cartons, rooms.

name: ROW
purpose: Returns the row number of a cell reference.

args.name: reference
args.desc: The cell to check; the formula's own cell if left out.

example.explain: Turns the sheet row of Meena into a serial number by subtracting the header row.

tip: =ROW()-1 in A2 filled down creates serial numbers that renumber after you delete rows.

name: ROWS
purpose: Returns the number of rows in a range or array.

args.name: array
args.desc: The range or array to count rows in.

example.explain: Counts the rows in the staff list, whether or not cells are filled.

tip: ROWS(A$2:A2) filled down gives a running count 1, 2, 3.

name: RRI
purpose: Returns the equivalent annual growth rate (CAGR) for an investment.

example.explain: Calculates the CAGR of a mutual fund that grew from 1 lakh to 1.8 lakh in 5 years.

tip: For investments with several deposits use XIRR instead of RRI.

name: RSQ
purpose: Returns the R-squared value of a linear regression line.

args.name: known_y's
args.desc: The dependent values, such as sales.

args.name: known_x's
args.desc: The independent values, such as ad spend.

example.explain: Shows how much of the change in sales is explained by ad spend.

tip: RSQ is simply CORREL squared.

name: RTD
purpose: Retrieves real-time data from a program that supports COM automation, such as a trading terminal.

args.name: progID
args.desc: The registered ID of the RTD server add-in, in quotes.

args.name: server
args.desc: The machine running the server; leave blank for your own computer.

args.name: topic1
args.desc: The first item of data to request, such as a symbol.

example.result: the live value sent by the RTD server
example.explain: Shows a live Nifty price from a broker's RTD add-in; it needs that add-in installed and registered, which most Indian trading terminals offer only on Windows.

tip: On a Mac, use STOCKHISTORY or the Stocks data type for delayed prices instead.

name: SCAN
purpose: Runs a LAMBDA over an array and returns every intermediate result, such as a running total.

args.name: initial_value
args.desc: The starting value of the accumulator.

args.name: lambda
args.desc: A LAMBDA with two parameters: the running value and the current value.

example.explain: Spills a cumulative year-to-date sales total for each month of the FY.

tip: Use REDUCE with the same LAMBDA when you only need the final total.

name: SEARCH
purpose: Returns the position of one text inside another, ignoring case and allowing wildcards.

args.name: find_text
args.desc: The text to look for; ? and * work as wildcards.

args.name: start_num
args.desc: Character position to start from; 1 if left out.

example.explain: Finds where the @ sits so you can split the name from the domain.

tip: =ISNUMBER(SEARCH("pune",A2)) is a neat case-free "contains" test.

name: SEARCHB
purpose: Returns the byte position of one text inside another, for double-byte languages.

example.explain: With English text each character is one byte, so it gives the same position as SEARCH.

tip: Use SEARCH unless a double-byte language is your default.

name: SEC
purpose: Returns the secant of an angle given in radians.

example.explain: The secant of 60 degrees (pi/3 radians) is 2.

name: SECH
purpose: Returns the hyperbolic secant of a number.

example.explain: Returns the hyperbolic secant of 1.

name: SECOND
purpose: Returns the seconds (0 to 59) from a time.

args.name: serial_number
args.desc: The time you want the seconds from.

example.explain: Pulls the seconds out of a biometric punch time.

name: SEQUENCE
purpose: Generates a list of sequential numbers as a spilled array.

args.name: columns
args.desc: How many columns to fill; 1 if left out.

args.name: start
args.desc: The first number; 1 if left out.

args.name: step
args.desc: How much to add each time; 1 if left out.

example.explain: Spills four invoice numbers starting at 1001.

tip: For a list of month-start dates use =EDATE(DATE(2026,4,1),SEQUENCE(12)-1), which gives April to March.

name: SERIESSUM
purpose: Returns the sum of a power series.

args.name: m
args.desc: How much the power goes up each term.

example.explain: Adds 1 + x + 0.5x² for x = 0.1, a close estimate of e to the power 0.1.

name: SHEET
purpose: Returns the position number of a sheet in the workbook.

args.name: value
args.desc: A sheet name or reference; the current sheet if left out.

example.explain: Shows that the formula sits on the first sheet of the workbook.

tip: =SHEET("Mar") tells you where a monthly sheet sits in the tab order.

name: SHEETS
purpose: Returns the number of sheets in a reference or in the whole workbook.

args.name: reference
args.desc: A 3-D reference to count sheets in; the whole workbook if left out.

example.explain: Counts the sheets in the workbook, which has just one here.

tip: =SHEETS(Apr:Mar!A1) counts the monthly sheets between two tabs.

name: SIGN
purpose: Tells you whether a number is positive, negative or zero by returning 1, -1 or 0.

example.explain: April shows a loss of ₹12,500, so SIGN returns -1.

tip: Combine with IF to label rows: =IF(SIGN(B2)<0,"Loss","Profit").

name: SIN
purpose: Returns the sine of an angle given in radians.

example.explain: Converts 30 degrees to radians and returns its sine, 0.5.

tip: Excel trig functions use radians, so wrap degrees in RADIANS first.

name: SINH
purpose: Returns the hyperbolic sine of a number.

example.explain: Returns the hyperbolic sine of 1.

name: SKEW
purpose: Measures how lopsided a sample of numbers is around its average.

example.explain: One very busy day (30 orders) pulls the tail to the right, so skewness is positive.

tip: Positive skew means a long tail of high values; check outliers before using the average.

name: SKEW.P
purpose: Measures how lopsided a whole population of numbers is around its average.

example.explain: Treats the five days as the full population and returns its skewness.

tip: Use SKEW for a sample and SKEW.P when the data is every value you care about.

name: SLN
purpose: Works out straight-line depreciation, the same amount every year.

args.name: salvage
args.desc: Value left at the end of its life

example.explain: A ₹5,00,000 machine worth ₹50,000 after 5 years loses ₹90,000 each year.

tip: Companies Act schedules often use written-down value; compare SLN with DB for the same asset.

name: SLOPE
purpose: Returns the slope of the best-fit straight line through your data, that is how much y changes for each unit of x.

args.name: known_y's
args.desc: The dependent values, such as sales

args.name: known_x's
args.desc: The independent values, such as ad spend

example.explain: Each extra ₹1,000 of ad spend goes with about ₹6,100 more sales.

tip: The y range comes first; swapping the ranges gives a different answer.

name: SMALL
purpose: Returns the k-th smallest value in a list, such as the second lowest quote.

args.name: k
args.desc: Position from the smallest (1 is the lowest)

example.explain: Returns the second lowest sales figure, Karan's ₹45,000.

tip: SMALL(range,1) is the same as MIN; use SEQUENCE for k to get the bottom 3 at once.

name: SORT
purpose: Sorts a range by a chosen column and spills the sorted list.

args.name: sort_index
args.desc: Which column (or row) to sort by; default 1

args.name: by_col
args.desc: TRUE to sort columns instead of rows

example.explain: Builds a leaderboard sorted by sales, highest first.

tip: The source stays untouched, so the sorted list updates when sales change; leave space below for the spill.

name: SORTBY
purpose: Sorts a range using the values in another range or column.

args.name: by_array2, sort_order2, ...
args.desc: More sort keys for tie breaks

example.explain: Lists only the names, ordered by their sales from highest to lowest.

tip: Unlike SORT, the sort column does not need to be part of what you return.

name: SQRT
purpose: Returns the square root of a positive number.

args.name: number
args.desc: The number whose square root you want

example.explain: A square plot of 1,600 sq ft is 40 ft on each side.

tip: A negative number gives #NUM!; wrap it in ABS if the sign does not matter.

name: SQRTPI
purpose: Returns the square root of a number multiplied by pi.

args.name: number
args.desc: The number to multiply by pi

example.explain: Returns the square root of pi times 1.

name: STANDARDIZE
purpose: Converts a value into a z-score, showing how many standard deviations it is from the average.

args.name: standard_dev
args.desc: The standard deviation of the data

example.explain: A test score of 82 is 1.5 standard deviations above the batch average.

tip: Z-scores let you compare marks or sales from groups with different averages.

name: STDEV
purpose: Older function for the standard deviation of a sample.

example.explain: Returns the sample standard deviation of branch sales, same as STDEV.S.

tip: Use STDEV.S in new workbooks; STDEV is kept only for compatibility.

name: STDEV.P
purpose: Returns the standard deviation when your data is the whole population.

example.explain: Treats these five branches as all the branches and measures how spread out their sales are.

tip: Use .P when you have every value (all branches); use .S when the data is a sample.

name: STDEV.S
purpose: Returns the standard deviation of a sample, a measure of how spread out the numbers are.

example.explain: Branch sales typically sit about ₹9.4 lakh away from the average of ₹48.6 lakh.

tip: Text and blank cells in the range are ignored; use STDEVA if text should count as zero.

name: STDEVA
purpose: Returns the sample standard deviation, counting text as 0 and TRUE as 1.

example.explain: Counts the absent learner as 0 when measuring the spread of scores.

tip: Only use the A versions when text really means zero; otherwise use STDEV.S.

name: STDEVP
purpose: Older function for the standard deviation of a whole population.

example.explain: Returns the population standard deviation of branch sales, same as STDEV.P.

tip: Use STDEV.P in new workbooks; STDEVP is kept only for compatibility.

name: STDEVPA
purpose: Returns the population standard deviation, counting text as 0 and TRUE as 1.

example.explain: Treats the four learners as the full group and counts Absent as 0.

name: STEYX
purpose: Returns the standard error of predicted y values in a straight-line regression.

example.explain: Shows that sales predicted from ad spend are typically off by about ₹3,000.

name: STOCKHISTORY
purpose: Fetches historical prices for a stock, fund or currency pair over a date range.

args.name: stock
args.desc: Ticker in quotes, such as "XNSE:TCS", or a Stocks data type cell

args.name: headers
args.desc: 0 none, 1 show headers (default), 2 headers with ticker

args.name: property0, ...
args.desc: Columns to return: 0 date, 1 close, 2 open, 3 high, 4 low, 5 volume

example.result: a table of dates and daily closing prices for TCS
example.explain: Needs Microsoft 365 and an internet connection; spills date and closing price for each trading day in the range.

tip: Use the XNSE: or XBOM: prefix so Excel picks the Indian listing, not a foreign one.

name: SUBSTITUTE
purpose: Replaces specific text with new text wherever it appears in a cell.

args.name: new_text
args.desc: The text to put in its place

args.name: instance_num
args.desc: Which occurrence to replace; all if left out

example.explain: Removes the hyphen so the mobile number is ten clean digits.

tip: SUBSTITUTE is case-sensitive; nest it to remove several characters, like spaces and hyphens.

name: SUBTOTAL
purpose: Calculates a total, count or average that can skip rows hidden by a filter.

args.name: function_num
args.desc: 1-11 includes manually hidden rows, 101-111 ignores them (9 or 109 is SUM); filtered-out rows are always skipped

example.explain: Adds the sales; if you filter to one region, the total changes to just the visible rows.

tip: Put SUBTOTAL above the header so it stays visible while you filter; SUBTOTALs inside the range are not double counted.

name: SUM
purpose: Adds up numbers, cells or ranges.

args.name: number1
args.desc: The first number, cell or range

args.name: number2, ...
args.desc: More numbers or ranges, up to 255

example.explain: Adds the three invoice lines to get the bill total before GST.

tip: Select the cell below a column and press ⌘ + Shift + T for AutoSum on a Mac.

name: SUMIF
purpose: Adds the values that meet one condition.

args.name: range
args.desc: Cells to test against the condition

args.name: sum_range
args.desc: Cells to add; if left out, range itself is added

example.explain: Adds sales only for rows where the region is North.

tip: Put the condition in a cell and refer to it, so one formula can be copied for every region.

name: SUMIFS
purpose: Adds the values that meet several conditions at once.

args.name: criteria_range1
args.desc: Cells to test for the first condition

example.explain: Adds sales for North in April only.

tip: Unlike SUMIF, the sum range comes first; all ranges must be the same size.

name: SUMPRODUCT
purpose: Multiplies matching items in ranges and adds up the results.

args.name: array2, ...
args.desc: More ranges of the same size

example.explain: Multiplies quantity by rate for each stationery item and totals the order value.

tip: Add conditions as multiplied tests, for example =SUMPRODUCT((A2:A4="Pens")*B2:B4*C2:C4).

name: SUMSQ
purpose: Returns the sum of the squares of the numbers.

example.explain: Squares 3 and 4 and adds them: 9 + 16 = 25.

name: SUMX2MY2
purpose: Adds up the differences between the squares of matching values in two ranges.

name: SUMX2PY2
purpose: Adds up the sums of the squares of matching values in two ranges.

name: SUMXMY2
purpose: Adds up the squares of the differences between matching values in two ranges.

example.explain: Each pair differs by 1, so the squared differences add to 3.

tip: Useful for the sum of squared errors between actual and forecast.

name: SWITCH
purpose: Compares one value against a list and returns the result for the first match.

args.name: value1
args.desc: The first value to compare with

args.name: result1
args.desc: What to return if it matches value1

args.name: default
args.desc: What to return if nothing matches

example.explain: Turns the short zone code N into the full name North.

tip: Always give a default, or unmatched codes return #N/A.

name: SYD
purpose: Works out sum-of-years' digits depreciation, which is higher in early years.

args.name: salvage
args.desc: Value left at the end of its life

example.explain: In year 1 the machine loses 5/15 of ₹4,50,000, which is ₹1,50,000.

name: T
purpose: Returns the value if it is text, and empty text if it is anything else.

args.name: value
args.desc: The value or cell to check

example.explain: A2 holds text, so T returns it; =T(A3) would return empty text because 2500 is a number.

tip: Rarely needed today; ISTEXT is clearer for checks.

name: T.DIST
purpose: Returns the left-tailed Student's t-distribution, used for small-sample tests.

args.name: cumulative
args.desc: TRUE for the cumulative probability, FALSE for the density

example.explain: Probability that a t value with 10 degrees of freedom is below 1.5.

name: T.DIST.2T
purpose: Returns the two-tailed Student's t-distribution probability.

example.explain: Two-tailed p-value for a t statistic of 2.1 with 15 degrees of freedom.

name: T.DIST.RT
purpose: Returns the right-tailed Student's t-distribution probability.

example.explain: One-tailed p-value for a t statistic of 2.1 with 15 degrees of freedom.

name: T.INV
purpose: Returns the t value for a given left-tailed probability.

example.explain: The t value below which 95% of a 10-degree-of-freedom distribution lies.

name: T.INV.2T
purpose: Returns the two-tailed t value for a given probability.

example.explain: Critical t value for a 95% two-sided confidence interval with 10 degrees of freedom.

name: T.TEST
purpose: Returns the probability that two samples come from groups with the same average.

example.explain: A small p-value suggests Pune's daily sales really are higher than Nagpur's, not just by chance.

tip: A result below 0.05 is the usual cut-off for a significant difference.

name: TAKE
purpose: Returns a set number of rows or columns from the start or end of a range.

args.name: rows
args.desc: Rows to keep; negative takes from the end

args.name: columns
args.desc: Columns to keep; negative takes from the end

example.explain: Keeps the top two rows of an already sorted list, a quick top 2.

tip: Pair with SORT for a live top N: =TAKE(SORT(A2:B5,2,-1),3).

name: TAN
purpose: Returns the tangent of an angle given in radians.

example.explain: The tangent of 45 degrees is 1.

tip: Convert degrees with RADIANS first.

name: TANH
purpose: Returns the hyperbolic tangent of a number.

example.explain: Returns the hyperbolic tangent of 0.5.

name: TBILLEQ
purpose: Returns the bond-equivalent yield of a Treasury bill.

args.name: maturity
args.desc: Date the bill matures (within a year)

example.explain: Converts a 6.5% discount on a 91-day T-bill into an equivalent bond yield.

name: TBILLPRICE
purpose: Returns the price per ₹100 face value of a Treasury bill.

example.explain: Price of a 91-day T-bill bought at a 6.5% discount.

name: TBILLYIELD
purpose: Returns the yield of a Treasury bill from its price.

example.explain: Annual yield earned on a 91-day T-bill bought at ₹98.40.

name: TDIST
purpose: Older function for the Student's t-distribution probability.

args.name: tails
args.desc: 1 for one tail, 2 for two tails

example.explain: Two-tailed probability for t = 2.1 with 15 degrees of freedom.

tip: Use T.DIST.2T or T.DIST.RT in new workbooks.

name: TEXT
purpose: Formats a number or date as text using a format code you choose.

args.name: value
args.desc: The number or date to format

args.name: format_text
args.desc: A format code in quotes, such as "dd-mmm-yyyy" or "#,##0"

example.explain: Puts a nicely formatted date inside a sentence instead of the serial number.

tip: Use "dd-mmm-yy" for 15-Aug-26 and "#,##0" for comma grouping; the format code must be in quotes.

name: TEXTAFTER
purpose: Returns the text that comes after a given character or word.

args.name: delimiter
args.desc: The character or word to split at

args.name: instance_num
args.desc: Which occurrence to use; negative counts from the end

args.name: match_end
args.desc: 1 treats the end of text as a delimiter

args.name: if_not_found
args.desc: What to return if the delimiter is missing

example.explain: Pulls the company domain out of an email address.

tip: Use -1 as instance_num to get the text after the last delimiter, like a file extension.

name: TEXTBEFORE
purpose: Returns the text that comes before a given character or word.

args.name: delimiter
args.desc: The character or word to split at

args.name: instance_num
args.desc: Which occurrence to use; negative counts from the end

args.name: match_end
args.desc: 1 treats the end of text as a delimiter

args.name: if_not_found
args.desc: What to return if the delimiter is missing

example.explain: Pulls the user name out of an email address.

tip: Without if_not_found, a missing delimiter gives #N/A.

name: TEXTJOIN
purpose: Joins text from many cells with a separator, and can skip blanks.

args.name: delimiter
args.desc: Text to put between items, such as ", "

example.explain: Makes one comma-separated list of cities and skips the empty cell.

tip: Pair with FILTER to list only matching items, for example all overdue invoice numbers.

name: TEXTSPLIT
purpose: Splits text into separate cells across columns or down rows using a delimiter.

args.name: col_delimiter
args.desc: Character that starts a new column

args.name: row_delimiter
args.desc: Character that starts a new row

example.explain: Splits a full name into first, middle and last name across three cells.

tip: It works on one cell at a time; for a whole column, use Text to Columns or BYROW.

name: TIME
purpose: Builds a time from separate hour, minute and second numbers.

args.name: minute
args.desc: Minute, extra minutes roll into hours

args.name: second
args.desc: Second, extra seconds roll into minutes

example.explain: Adds a 75-minute break to a 9:30 start, giving 10:45.

tip: Format the result as hh:mm, otherwise you will see a decimal like 0.448.

name: TIMEVALUE
purpose: Converts a time typed as text into a real Excel time.

args.name: time_text
args.desc: Text that looks like a time, such as "09:45"

example.explain: Turns a punch-in time exported as text into a time you can subtract from punch-out.

tip: The result is a decimal fraction of a day; apply a time format to see 09:45.

name: TINV
purpose: Older function for the two-tailed inverse of the t-distribution.

example.explain: Critical t value for a two-sided test at 5% with 10 degrees of freedom.

tip: Use T.INV.2T in new workbooks.

name: TOCOL
purpose: Turns a block of cells into a single column.

args.name: ignore
args.desc: 0 keep all (default), 1 skip blanks, 2 skip errors, 3 skip both

example.explain: Reads the grid row by row and stacks all values into one column.

tip: Use ignore = 1 to drop blanks when combining uneven lists.

name: TODAY
purpose: Returns today's date, updating every time the sheet recalculates.

example.explain: Shows the current date, so the result changes every day.

tip: Press ⌘ + ; to type a fixed date that will not change.

name: TOROW
purpose: Turns a block of cells into a single row.

args.name: ignore
args.desc: 0 keep all (default), 1 skip blanks, 2 skip errors, 3 skip both

example.explain: Lays all four values out in one row.

name: TRANSLATE
purpose: Translates text from one language to another using Microsoft's translation service.

args.name: source_language
args.desc: Language code of the text, such as "en"; detected if left out

args.name: target_language
args.desc: Language code to translate into, such as "hi"; defaults to your system language

example.explain: Needs Microsoft 365 and an internet connection; translates English feedback into Hindi (exact wording may vary).

tip: Give the source language for short text; there is a daily limit, after which you see a throttled error.

name: TRANSPOSE
purpose: Flips a range so rows become columns and columns become rows.

example.explain: Turns a month-wise row layout into a column layout.

tip: In Microsoft 365 it spills on its own; in older Excel select the target and press ⌘ + Shift + Return.

name: TREND
purpose: Predicts values along a straight-line trend fitted to your data.

args.name: known_y's
args.desc: The values you already have, such as sales

args.name: known_x's
args.desc: Matching x values, such as month numbers

args.name: new_x's
args.desc: The x values to predict for

args.name: const
args.desc: FALSE forces the line through zero

example.explain: Projects month 5 sales of about ₹1,77,500 from the straight-line trend.

tip: Give several new x values to forecast many months in one spill.

name: TRIM
purpose: Removes extra spaces, leaving single spaces between words.

example.explain: Cleans leading, trailing and double spaces from a name.

tip: TRIM does not remove non-breaking spaces from web data; use SUBSTITUTE(A2,CHAR(160)," ") first.

name: TRIMMEAN
purpose: Returns the average after dropping a percentage of the highest and lowest values.

args.name: percent
args.desc: Fraction of points to drop in total, split equally between top and bottom

example.explain: Drops the fastest and the slowest delivery, then averages 3, 3 and 4.

tip: Good for averages that one freak value would distort, like a delayed shipment.

name: TRIMRANGE
purpose: Trims empty rows and columns from the edges of a range so formulas only see the used part.

args.name: trim_rows
args.desc: 0 none, 1 leading blanks, 2 trailing blanks, 3 both (default)

args.name: trim_cols
args.desc: 0 none, 1 leading blanks, 2 trailing blanks, 3 both (default)

example.explain: Returns only the filled rows, dropping the blank rows at the bottom.

tip: The shortcut A2:.A1000 does the same trim inside any formula.

name: TRUE
purpose: Returns the logical value TRUE.

example.explain: Returns TRUE; you can also just type TRUE in a cell or formula.

tip: In maths TRUE counts as 1, so =TRUE()+TRUE() gives 2.

name: TRUNC
purpose: Cuts a number to a set number of decimals without rounding.

example.explain: Keeps one decimal and simply drops the rest, without rounding up.

tip: For negatives TRUNC and INT differ: TRUNC(-4.7) is -4, INT(-4.7) is -5.

name: TTEST
purpose: Older function for the probability from a Student's t-test.

example.explain: Same result as T.TEST for the two branches' daily sales.

tip: Use T.TEST in new workbooks.

name: TYPE
purpose: Returns a number that tells you what kind of value a cell holds.

example.explain: Returns 2 because the cell holds text (1 number, 4 logical, 16 error, 64 array).

name: UNICHAR
purpose: Returns the character for a Unicode number.

example.explain: Code 8377 is the Indian rupee sign.

tip: Handy for symbols like ✓ (10003) in reports.

name: UNICODE
purpose: Returns the Unicode number of the first character of text.

example.explain: Shows the code number for the rupee sign.

tip: Use it to identify a stray invisible character, such as 160 for a non-breaking space.

name: UNIQUE
purpose: Returns a list of the distinct values in a range.

args.name: by_col
args.desc: TRUE compares columns instead of rows

args.name: exactly_once
args.desc: TRUE returns only values that appear once

example.explain: Builds a customer list with each name only once.

tip: Wrap in SORT for an alphabetical list: =SORT(UNIQUE(A2:A6)).

name: UPPER
